accept-vs-except-take-in-vs-leave-out.context_blurb:
Accept and except sound almost identical and mean opposite things. Accept is a verb: to take something in, to agree to it, to receive it. Except nearly always means leaving something out, and it works like a tiny version of but.

The syllables carry the hint. Accept begins like acquire, and acquiring means taking in. Except begins like exit and exclude, and both of those head out the door. So if the sentence lets something in, use the first word; if it fences something off, use the second.

Example: 'Dad accepted every excuse except the one about the dog.' He took in all the excuses, and one was left out. Swap the two words and you get 'Dad excepted every excuse accept the one about the dog', which says he excluded the whole lot and then stops making sense. One rarer use is worth knowing: 'except that' can stand in for but at the front of a clause, as in 'I would have come, except that the bus never arrived.'
accept-vs-except-take-in-vs-leave-out.title: Accept vs Except — Take in vs Leave Out

active-vs-passive-voice-when-the-actor-m.context_blurb:
An active sentence puts the doer first: subject, then verb, then object. A passive sentence promotes the object to subject and pushes the doer into a by phrase, or drops him altogether. The test is quick. Ask who did it, then see whether the sentence bothers to tell you.

Passive is not a mistake. It earns its place when the doer is unknown, obvious or genuinely beside the point, as in 'The bridge was built in 1883.' It turns sneaky when a writer uses it to bury a name that ought to be printed, which is why official apologies so often report that errors occurred and never say whose.

Example: 'The window was broken' tells you about a window. 'My brother broke the window' tells you whom to send the bill to. Both are perfectly grammatical English, and only one of them assigns the blame. Choose active whenever responsibility or speed matters, and keep passive for the sentences where the doer really does not belong in the spotlight.
active-vs-passive-voice-when-the-actor-m.title: Active vs Passive Voice: When the Actor Matters

affect-vs-effect-verb-vs-noun-usually.context_blurb:
Nine times out of ten, affect is the verb and effect is the noun. Something affects you, and what follows is an effect. The mnemonic RAVEN exists for exactly this pair: the A word is the verb, the E word is the noun.

Two exceptions are worth knowing, because both are real English. Used as a verb, to effect means to bring about, as in 'the new mayor effected a change in the bus routes'. Used as a noun, affect is the term doctors reach for when describing a patient's visible emotion, as in 'a flat affect'.

Example: 'Loud music affects my homework, and the result is a bad grade.' Test yourself by swapping in a plain substitute. If the word influences fits the slot, write affect. If the word result fits, write effect. That one swap settles almost every sentence you will ever write.
affect-vs-effect-verb-vs-noun-usually.title: Affect vs Effect — Verb vs Noun (Usually)

anaphora-and-epistrophe-repetition-at-th.context_blurb:
Three repetition figures are easy to tell apart once you know where to listen. Anaphora is repetition at the front, where one clause after another opens with the same words, the way Churchill's wartime speech kept opening with 'we shall fight'. Epistrophe is its mirror image, repeating the same words at the close of phrase after phrase, as Lincoln's final line at Gettysburg does with 'the people'. Anadiplosis is a relay race: the word that ends one clause starts the next one.

When a passage does the opening trick and the closing trick at the same time, the name for the double pattern is symploce.

Example: 'Every night he practised. Every night he failed. Every night he started again.' The opening words repeat, so that is anaphora. Rewrite it as 'he practised all night, he failed all night, he started again all night' and the repeated words have moved to the end, which makes it epistrophe. Listen for the position, not for the words.
anaphora-and-epistrophe-repetition-at-th.title: Anaphora and Epistrophe: Repetition at the Start, Repetition at the End

apostrophes-in-contractions-and-not-in-p.context_blurb:
An apostrophe in a contraction stands in for letters you dropped. Do not becomes don't, we are becomes we're, cannot becomes can't, and in each one the mark sits exactly where a letter went missing. Possession is the other legitimate job, as in the dog's bowl.

What an apostrophe never does is make a plural. A shop sign reading APPLE'S 1 POUND is the famous greengrocer's apostrophe, and it promises one apple that owns a pound. Decades behave the same way, so write the 1970s and the 1990s with no mark at all. Single letters are the one surviving exception, because as and is would look like words, so you dot your i's and cross your t's.

Example: 'The cat's toys are everywhere' says the toys belong to one cat. 'The cat's are everywhere' says nothing at all, because the apostrophe has turned a simple plural into a possessive that never finishes.
apostrophes-in-contractions-and-not-in-p.title: Apostrophes in Contractions and NOT in Plurals or Decades

appositive-commas-my-brother-mark-vs-my-.context_blurb:
An appositive is a noun or phrase dropped in beside another noun to rename it. Whether it takes commas depends on one question: would the sentence still point at the right person without it?

If the extra information is merely extra, fence it off with a pair of commas. If it is doing the pointing, leave the commas off. That is why punctuation quietly reports on your family. 'My sister, Rosa, baked the cake' says there is exactly one sister and her name is thrown in as a bonus. 'My sister Rosa baked the cake' admits to several sisters and names the one who did the baking.

Example: 'Our dog, Scout, chewed the remote' claims a single dog. 'Our dog Scout chewed the remote' quietly confesses to a kennel. Say both aloud. The comma version has a small pause on either side, and that pause is the signal that the name could be lifted out without damaging the sentence.
appositive-commas-my-brother-mark-vs-my-.title: Appositive Commas: 'My Brother Mark' vs 'My Brother, Mark'

backronym-the-acronym-invented-after-the.context_blurb:
Three word-building labels get tangled together. An acronym takes the initials of a phrase and is said as a word, like NASA or radar. An initialism takes initials too but is spelled out letter by letter, like FBI or HTML. A backronym runs the whole process backwards: the word already exists, and somebody later invents a phrase to fit its letters.

Backronyms travel as folk history, which is why so many of them sound too tidy to be true. Golf is centuries older than the claim that it stands for Gentlemen Only, Ladies Forbidden. SOS was chosen in 1906 because its Morse pattern is impossible to mistake, long before anyone explained it as Save Our Souls. Meredith G. Williams coined the word backronym itself for a Washington Post reader contest in 1983, out of back plus acronym.

Example: a sign claims that TIP means To Insure Promptness. The tip came first and the phrase was fitted around it afterwards, so the phrase is an invention rather than an origin.
backronym-the-acronym-invented-after-the.title: Backronym: The Acronym Invented AFTER the Word

bare-vs-bear-naked-vs-the-animal.context_blurb:
Bare means uncovered, empty, nothing on it. Bear is both the animal and a verb meaning to carry or to endure. The spelling hint is the vowel: bare has the A of naked, and a bare cupboard has nothing inside it.

Bear does all the heavy lifting. A beam bears a roof, a witness bears witness, a tree bears fruit, and a patient girl bears an annoying brother. That is why 'bear with me' is the right form when you ask somebody to wait. Write 'bare with me' and you have invited him to take his clothes off instead.

Example: 'The pantry was bare, so the hiker had to bear his own food up the hill.' The pantry had nothing in it; the hiker carried the load. The two words sound identical, so meaning is the only test available. Ask whether the sentence is about emptiness or about carrying, and spell accordingly.
bare-vs-bear-naked-vs-the-animal.title: Bare vs Bear — Naked vs the Animal

between-vs-among-two-vs-more-than-two.context_blurb:
The rule taught in school is a head count: between for two things, among for three or more. 'Choose between the red door and the blue door' takes two, while 'she wandered among the trees' takes a whole forest.

The real rule is sharper than counting, and it explains the exceptions. Between is for one-to-one relationships, however many parties are involved. Among is for a mass you never divide up. That is why a treaty signed by five nations is still between them: every signer deals separately with every other signer. A jury that talks as one body deliberates among its members.

Example: 'The money was split between the twins' gives each twin a named share. 'The money was spread among the crowd' means nobody is counting heads. Remember also that both words are prepositions, so the pronoun after either one takes its object form: a secret stays between you and me, never between you and I.
between-vs-among-two-vs-more-than-two.title: Between vs Among: Two vs More Than Two

between-you-and-i-the-pronoun-after-prep.context_blurb:
A preposition takes an object, so the pronoun that follows it must be in object form: me, him, her, us and them. 'Between you and I' breaks that rule, and it breaks it out of politeness. People get corrected for saying me so often that I starts to feel like the dressed-up version, and grammarians call that hypercorrection.

The fix takes one second. Drop the other person and listen. Nobody says between I. Nobody says for I. Put the other name back in and the pronoun does not change.

Example: 'Grandma sent a card to my brother and ___.' Take the brother out and you get 'Grandma sent a card to me', so the finished sentence reads 'to my brother and me'. The same test retires myself, which is reflexive and needs an earlier I in the same sentence. 'I hurt myself' is fine. 'The coach thanked my dad and myself' should simply end in me.
between-you-and-i-the-pronoun-after-prep.title: Between You and I: The Pronoun-After-Preposition Trap

block-quotes-and-dialogue-tag-punctuatio.context_blurb:
Dialogue punctuation is a small set of habits. When the tag comes first, a comma goes before the opening quotation mark: She said, "Follow me." When the tag comes afterwards, that final period becomes a comma and stays inside the closing mark: "Follow me," she said. In American style, commas and periods always sit inside the quotation marks.

Capital letters follow sentences, not quotation marks. If one sentence of speech ends and a second begins, the second starts with a capital even though it is still inside the quotation. A long quotation is set as a block instead, indented, with no quotation marks around it at all. Chicago suggests that treatment for runs of about a hundred words or more, for five or more lines of verse, and for an exchange of dialogue. In a novel, a fresh paragraph is enough to tell the reader that a new person is talking.

Example: "Wait here," Dad said. "I forgot the keys." One comma inside, one period inside, and a capital letter on the new sentence.
block-quotes-and-dialogue-tag-punctuatio.title: Block Quotes and Dialogue Tag Punctuation

breath-vs-breathe-noun-vs-verb.context_blurb:
Breath is the thing; breathe is the doing. The extra E on the end marks the verb, and it changes the sound as well, since breath rhymes with death while breathe rhymes with seethe. Say the sentence aloud and the right spelling usually picks itself.

A noun slot wants the short form. You take a breath, you hold your breath, you waste your breath. A verb slot wants the long one. You breathe in, you breathe out, you breathe through your nose. The same noun-and-verb pattern turns up elsewhere. A wreath hangs on a door, and mist can wreathe a mountain. A bath is a thing, and to bathe is an action.

Example: 'He held his breath for a minute, then started to breathe again.' The first slot names something he held, so no E goes on the end. The second names something he did, so the E goes on.
breath-vs-breathe-noun-vs-verb.title: Breath vs Breathe — Noun vs Verb

british-vs-american-spelling-colour-thea.context_blurb:
British and American spelling split along a few predictable seams. Britain keeps the U in colour, honour and labour, and America drops it. Britain writes theatre, centre and metre, and America flips those endings to theater, center and meter. Britain often prefers the S in organise and apologise, while America uses the Z every time, though even in Britain the Oxford house style favours the Z. Some pairs are nothing but regional taste: gray and grey are both real spellings, and neither one is an error.

The rule that actually matters in your own writing is not which system you pick but that you stay inside it. Mixing the two reads as carelessness rather than style.

Example: 'The theatre's colour scheme is grey' is consistently British. 'The theater's color scheme is gray' is consistently American. 'The theater's colour scheme is grey' is a muddle, because it has borrowed one ending from each side of the Atlantic.
british-vs-american-spelling-colour-thea.title: British vs American Spelling — Colour, Theatre, Gray

buffalo-buffalo-the-sentence-that-uses-o.context_blurb:
The famous eight-word sentence 'Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo' really is English, and it works because a single spelling carries three separate jobs. Buffalo is a city in New York state, a buffalo is the animal, and to buffalo somebody is to bully him. William J. Rapaport made the puzzle famous in a note from 1972, written while he was at the State University of New York at Buffalo.

Shorter versions are easier to hear. 'Fish fish fish' parses as fish that other fish catch go catching themselves. Four buffalo in a row say that bison from that city bully other bison from the same place.

Example: build the trick yourself with a word that is both a noun and a verb. 'Police police police' means officers whom other officers supervise do some supervising of their own. Once your ear can sort out which copy is a name, which is a creature and which is an action, the long version stops looking like a typing accident.
buffalo-buffalo-the-sentence-that-uses-o.title: Buffalo Buffalo: The Sentence That Uses One Word Eight Ways

can-vs-may-ability-vs-permission.context_blurb:
In the strict rule, can asks about ability and may asks about permission. That is the joke behind the oldest exchange in school: a student asks whether he can leave the room, and the teacher answers that he does not know, is the student able? The boy had the ability all along. What he wanted was permission.

Informal English stopped keeping the two apart more than a century ago, so asking whether you can have a cookie is ordinary modern speech. In a formal letter, an interview or an exam, may still sounds correct and can sounds careless. Might is the softer cousin, reporting a possibility rather than asking for anything.

Example: 'Can he lift that box?' asks about his muscles. 'May he lift that box?' asks whether he is allowed to touch it. Same box, two completely different questions, and the verb is the only thing that tells them apart.
can-vs-may-ability-vs-permission.title: Can vs May: Ability vs Permission

capital-vs-capitol-the-city-the-money-th.context_blurb:
Capital with an A does nearly every job in the language: the city where a government sits, money put into a business, a capital letter, and the adjective in capital punishment. Capitol with an O does exactly one job. It names the building where lawmakers meet, and nothing else.

The O is the memory hook, because a capitol usually wears a dome and a dome is round. The name traces back to the Capitoline Hill in Rome, where the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus once stood.

Example: 'Sacramento is the capital of California, and the capitol downtown has a golden dome.' The first word names a city, so it takes the A. The second names a legislative building, so it takes the O. If your sentence is not about a specific legislature's building, the A spelling is almost certainly the one you want.
capital-vs-capitol-the-city-the-money-th.title: Capital vs Capitol — The City, the Money, the Building

capitalization-at-sentence-start-and-aft.context_blurb:
Capital letters mark beginnings, not punctuation marks. The first word of a sentence takes one, and so does the first word of a full sentence quoted inside it, which means both rules fire at once when a tag comes first.

After a colon, house styles disagree, and it is worth knowing which one you are following. Chicago leaves the next word lowercase unless what follows is a quotation or runs to more than one sentence. Associated Press style capitalises whenever a complete sentence follows the colon. Either is defensible; mixing them inside one essay is not. Titles run on their own system. Title case capitalises the first word, the last word and the important words in between, leaving short articles and prepositions alone.

Example: 'he shouted, "come back!"' is missing two capitals, one for the sentence and one for the speech, and should read 'He shouted, "Come back!"' A family word takes a capital only when it stands in for a name, so write 'Grandpa is late' but 'my grandpa is late'.
capitalization-at-sentence-start-and-aft.title: Capitalization at Sentence Start and After Colons

chiasmus-the-mirror-image-sentence.context_blurb:
Chiasmus is a mirror. The second half of the line repeats the first half with the key pair of words in reverse order, and the crossing shape gives it the name: the Greek letter chi is written like an X. John F. Kennedy closed his inaugural address on January 20, 1961 with the most quoted one in American speech, telling the country to ask not what it could do for them but what they could do for it. The two halves trade places, and the trade is the whole effect.

Do not confuse it with anaphora, which simply repeats the same opening words clause after clause and reverses nothing.

Example: 'He eats to live, not lives to eat.' The verbs eat and live swap positions, so the line is a chiasmus. 'He eats quickly, he eats loudly, he eats constantly' repeats an opening instead, which makes it anaphora. Test any candidate by asking whether anything actually crossed over.
chiasmus-the-mirror-image-sentence.title: Chiasmus: The Mirror-Image Sentence

collective-nouns-team-family-jury-us-vs-.context_blurb:
A collective noun names one group made of many members: team, family, jury, committee, staff. American English treats the group as a single unit, so the verb and the pronoun both stay singular. The team is winning. The jury has reached its verdict.

British English allows the plural when the members are clearly acting separately, which is why a British paper can print that the team are arguing. American writers reach for the plural only in that same situation, and even then it usually reads better to name the members outright: the jurors disagree. Two traps sit nearby. A measurement takes a singular verb, because the amount is one thing, so two hundred miles is a long drive. And the phrase 'a number of' is plural in meaning, so a number of students are absent, even though the word number looks singular all by itself.

Example: 'The family is driving to the coast' moves one car. 'The family members are packing separately' makes the individuals visible, which is the cleanest fix of all in American English.
collective-nouns-team-family-jury-us-vs-.title: Collective Nouns: Team, Family, Jury (US vs UK)

colons-in-time-ratios-and-bible-referenc.context_blurb:
Besides introducing a list, the colon works as a plain separator between two numbers, and in that job it never takes a space on either side. Clock time puts hours on the left and minutes on the right, as in 3:45 in the afternoon. Odds and ratios use the same shape, so two to one is written 2:1. Chapter-and-verse references in the Bible follow the pattern too, with the chapter first and the verse after.

A colon also divides a book's title from its subtitle, and American style capitalises the first word that follows it.

Example: 'The bus leaves at 7:05, and the sign gives the hill's slope as 1:12.' Neither colon has a space around it, and neither one is introducing anything. For a span of verses, keep the single colon and use a dash for the range, so the twenty-third psalm from verse 1 through verse 6 is written 23:1-6.
colons-in-time-ratios-and-bible-referenc.title: Colons in Time, Ratios, and Bible References

colons-introducing-lists-quotes-and-expl.context_blurb:
A colon promises that something is coming: a list, a quotation, or an explanation of what was just said. The one condition is that whatever sits in front of the colon must already be a complete sentence on its own.

That single condition kills the commonest mistake. 'She packed three things: a book, a hat and snacks' is right, because the words before the mark stand alone. 'She packed: a book, a hat and snacks' is wrong, because 'she packed' is still waiting for its object and the colon has cut it off from the only words that finish it. The repair is usually to delete the colon rather than to add anything.

Example: 'He had one goal: to finish before dark.' Everything before the mark is a sentence, and everything after it explains the goal. Swap in a comma and the promise disappears. Keep the colon, and the reader knows that something is about to arrive.
colons-introducing-lists-quotes-and-expl.title: Colons: Introducing Lists, Quotes, and Explanations

comma-before-a-coordinating-conjunction-.context_blurb:
Seven short words join two complete sentences as equals, and the mnemonic FANBOYS holds all of them: for, and, nor, but, or, yet and so. When one of the seven links two full clauses, put a comma in front of it.

That comma does real work. It warns the reader that a second subject and verb are on the way. If the words after the conjunction are not a full clause, leave the comma out. Chicago also lets you drop it when both halves are very short and tightly linked. Watch out for words that merely look like conjunctions. However, therefore and moreover are adverbs, so they need a semicolon or a full stop in front of them, never a bare comma.

Example: 'The power failed, and the freezer thawed' has two clauses, so it takes the comma. 'The power failed and stayed off all night' has one subject doing two things, so it takes none at all.
comma-before-a-coordinating-conjunction-.title: Comma Before a Coordinating Conjunction (FANBOYS)

comma-splices-two-sentences-joined-only-.context_blurb:
A comma splice happens when a comma, all on its own, is asked to join two sentences that could each stand alone. 'The sun rose, birds began singing' is a splice: two complete sentences with one weak mark between them.

There are four honest repairs. Use a full stop. Use a semicolon. Add one of the FANBOYS conjunctions after the comma. Or make one half depend on the other with a word like because or when. Deleting the comma is not a repair, because then the sentences run straight together into a fused sentence, which reads worse. The usual trap is a word like however, therefore or moreover. These feel like joiners but behave as adverbs, so a comma in front of one still leaves a splice, and a semicolon is what fixes it.

Example: 'My brother forgot the tickets, we waited outside.' Put a semicolon in the gap, or write 'so we waited outside', and the sentence is sound again.
comma-splices-two-sentences-joined-only-.title: Comma Splices: Two Sentences Joined ONLY by a Comma

commas-in-addresses-springfield-illinois.context_blurb:
A state or country name after a city behaves like an appositive, so it needs a comma on both sides whenever the sentence keeps going. Most writers remember the first comma and forget the second one, and that forgotten mark is the whole mistake.

'She grew up in Dayton, Ohio, and moved east' is right: one comma after the city, one after the state. Drop the second and the state starts leaning on the rest of the sentence. If the place name lands at the very end, the full stop does the closing comma's job instead. Inside a mailing address, the postal code is the exception, because no comma stands between a state and the number that follows it.

Example: 'Our cousins in Austin, Texas, send cookies in December.' Lift the state out and the sentence still works, which is the sign that the pair of commas is right. A city famous enough to need no explaining travels alone, so 'she lives in Paris' needs nothing added.
commas-in-addresses-springfield-illinois.title: Commas in Addresses: 'Springfield, Illinois'

commas-in-dates-july-4-1776-was-independ.context_blurb:
In the American month-day-year form, the year behaves like an appositive and takes a comma on each side. 'The surrender was signed on April 9, 1865, in a farmhouse' carries one comma before the year and one after it. When the date ends the sentence, the full stop covers the second position, so only a single comma shows.

Two other forms take no comma at all. A month with a year but no day needs none, as in July 1776. The day-month-year order used across Europe and in the military needs none either, because nothing is interrupting anything, as in 4 July 1776.

Example: 'She was born on March 2, 2009, in a snowstorm' keeps both commas. 'She was born on March 2, 2009.' keeps one. 'She was born in March 2009' keeps none. Between two full dates, Chicago asks for an en dash rather than more commas.
commas-in-dates-july-4-1776-was-independ.title: Commas in Dates: 'July 4, 1776, Was Independence Day'

common-misspellings-separate-definitely-.context_blurb:
Most notorious misspellings fail in one of two places: a vowel in the middle, or a doubled consonant. Both have cures.

For the vowel, hunt for a smaller word hiding inside the long one. A rat sits in the middle of separate, which settles the second A. Finite hides inside definitely, which settles the I. Leg finishes privilege, so no D sneaks in, and rhythm has no spare vowel to lose at all. For the consonants, learn the pattern instead of the word. Accommodate doubles both its C and its M. Embarrass doubles both the R and the S. Occur keeps single letters until you add an ending, which doubles the R. Necessary is the odd one out, with a single C but a pair of S's.

Example: spell millennium by splitting it into its Latin pieces, mille for a thousand and annus for a year. Each piece keeps its own double letter, which gives you two Ls and then two Ns in the middle.
common-misspellings-separate-definitely-.title: Common Misspellings — Separate, Definitely, Accommodate

compared-to-vs-compared-with.context_blurb:
The strict distinction is about what kind of comparison you are making. Compared to points at a likeness between things of different kinds, which is the job a metaphor does. Compared with sets two things of the same kind side by side and runs down the differences item by item.

Shakespeare's eighteenth sonnet opens by comparing a person to a summer's day, and that is the analogy sense, since a human being and a day are not the same sort of thing. A scientist lining one group of patients up against another is doing the other job, which is why formal papers keep with. Honesty about the rule matters here. Outside formal science writing, almost nobody observes the distinction any more, and both prepositions turn up in both roles. Knowing it is still useful, because it tells you what a careful writer meant.

Example: 'Her voice compared to a trumpet' praises her by analogy. 'Her voice compared with last year's recording' promises a measured before and after.
compared-to-vs-compared-with.title: Compared to vs Compared with

complement-vs-compliment-completing-vs-p.context_blurb:
Complement with an E completes something. Compliment with an I is praise. The spelling hook sits in the middle of each word: complEment shares its PLE with complEte, while the I in complIment stands for the I who says 'I like it'.

Complement is also a noun, and it turns up in two different school subjects. In grammar it is the word that finishes what a linking verb started, so in 'she is a teacher' the job title does the finishing. In geometry two angles are complementary when the pair adds up to a right angle.

Example: 'He paid her a compliment, and the gravy complemented the roast.' One is spoken praise; the other is a thing that completes a dish. Test it by swapping in a plain word. If praise fits the slot, spell it with an I. If completes fits, spell it with an E.
complement-vs-compliment-completing-vs-p.title: Complement vs Compliment — Completing vs Praising

compound-subjects-with-and-usually-plura.context_blurb:
Two subjects joined by and normally add up to a plural, so they take a plural verb. My brother and my sister are coming over. The blanket and the pillow are on the bed.

The exception sounds wrong until you see why it works. When the two words name one single thing rather than two, the subject is singular. Macaroni and cheese is one dish, not two foods standing side by side, so it takes a singular verb. The same goes for bacon and eggs when you mean the breakfast. The test is whether you can point at one thing or two. Salt and pepper are on the table, because there are two shakers to pick up. But peanut butter and jelly is his favourite sandwich, because there is one sandwich on the plate.

Example: 'Fish and chips is cheap on Fridays' orders a single meal. 'The fish and the chips are getting cold' complains about two separate items, and the repeated article in front of each noun is the giveaway.
compound-subjects-with-and-usually-plura.title: Compound Subjects with AND: Usually Plural, Sometimes Singular

compound-subjects-with-or-nor-the-nearer.context_blurb:
When or or nor joins two subjects, the verb does not add them up. It agrees with whichever subject sits closer to it. That is the nearer-subject rule, and it explains how two sentences built from the same words can take different verbs.

The dog or the cats are hungry, because cats stands nearest. Flip the order, and the cats or the dog is hungry, because dog now stands nearest. Nor follows the same pattern: neither the students nor the teacher knows, while neither the teacher nor the students know. This is the opposite of how and behaves, since and makes a plural whatever the order.

Example: 'Either my cousins or my uncle ___ driving.' The nearer subject is uncle, which is singular, so the verb is 'is driving'. Put the uncle first and the sentence becomes 'Either my uncle or my cousins are driving'. Writers who dislike the lopsided result simply reorder the pair so the plural lands beside the verb, or choose a verb form that fits both subjects.
compound-subjects-with-or-nor-the-nearer.title: Compound Subjects with OR/NOR: The Nearer-Subject Rule

comprise-vs-compose-the-whole-includes-t.context_blurb:
Comprise and compose run in opposite directions. The whole comprises its parts, and the parts compose the whole. A substitution test settles nearly every case: if includes or contains fits the slot, you want comprise; if the words make up fit, you want compose.

So a committee comprises twelve members, and twelve members compose the committee. The phrase careful editors object to is 'comprised of', because it turns comprise around and dresses the whole up as the parts. Write 'is composed of' or simply 'comprises' instead. Nobody objects to 'composed of', which has always carried that preposition.

Example: 'The album comprises ten songs' is clean, and 'ten songs compose the album' says the same thing from the other end. 'The album is comprised of ten songs' is the version a copy-editor will strike through. Ordinary usage is drifting towards it, but the formal style guides still hold the line.
comprise-vs-compose-the-whole-includes-t.title: Comprise vs Compose — The Whole Includes the Parts

concision-eliminating-deadwood-phrases.context_blurb:
Deadwood is any phrase that spends four words doing one word's job. Cutting it is not about writing short sentences; it is about making every word carry weight.

Learn the standard swaps. 'Due to the fact that' is just because. 'In the event that' is just if. 'In a careful manner' is carefully. 'At this point in time' is now. Openers like 'it is important to note that' and frames like 'there are ... who' can usually be deleted outright, because the sentence underneath them was already complete. Watch for redundant pairs as well, since a gift is free by definition and 'exact same' says same twice over.

Example: 'The reason why he was late is because the bus broke down' carries two redundancies at once, as 'the reason why' and 'is because' both announce a cause. Trim it to 'he was late because the bus broke down' and nothing has been lost except seven words.
concision-eliminating-deadwood-phrases.title: Concision: Eliminating Deadwood Phrases

contractions-in-formal-writing.context_blurb:
A contraction is not an error. It is a register signal. Don't, can't and it's tell a reader that the writing is relaxed, which is exactly right in dialogue, a personal essay, a blog post or most journalism.

Formal writing expands them. A research paper, a lab report, a legal letter or a job application writes do not, cannot and it is. The reason is tone rather than logic: the full forms sound measured, and a cover letter that opens with slang and contractions reads as though the writer did not take the occasion seriously. The test is to read the sentence out loud. If it sounds like a friend talking across a table, keep the contraction. If it sounds like something being presented to a committee, spell both words out.

Example: 'We didn't find any effect' belongs in conversation. 'We did not find any effect' belongs in the write-up, and nothing else in the sentence has to change.
contractions-in-formal-writing.title: Contractions in Formal Writing

contronym-the-word-that-means-its-own-op.context_blurb:
A contronym is a single word that can mean its own opposite. Some writers call it a Janus word, after the Roman god whose two faces looked in opposite directions.

Cleave is the classic. A cleaver cleaves meat in two, splitting it apart, while the old wedding vow has a husband cleave to his wife, clinging to her. Sanction can approve a plan or punish a country. Dust can mean adding powder to a cake or wiping powder off a shelf. Oversight can mean careful supervision or a careless mistake. Trim can mean adding decoration to a coat or cutting cloth away from it. Only the surrounding words decide which sense is live, which makes a contronym a gift to a joke and a hazard in a set of instructions.

Example: 'The ship was bound for Dover, and the cargo was bound with rope.' One bound is heading somewhere; the other is tied up tight. Same five letters, opposite jobs, one sentence.
contronym-the-word-that-means-its-own-op.title: Contronym: The Word That Means Its Own Opposite

coordinate-adjective-commas-a-small-red-.context_blurb:
Two adjectives in front of a noun come in two kinds. Coordinate adjectives each modify the noun on their own, and a comma goes between them. Cumulative adjectives stack up, each one modifying everything that follows it, and they take no comma at all.

Two quick tests sort them out. Put and between the pair, then swap their order. If both versions still sound like English, the adjectives are coordinate and the comma belongs, which is why a bright, sunny day survives as bright and sunny and as sunny and bright. If either test produces nonsense, leave the comma out, which is why nobody punctuates a small red ball. English also has a fixed order for stacked adjectives that native speakers follow without ever being taught it: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, then purpose. Because that order is doing the work, stacked adjectives rarely need commas.

Example: 'a cold, miserable afternoon' passes both tests, so it keeps the comma. 'an old wooden gate' fails both, so it keeps none.
coordinate-adjective-commas-a-small-red-.title: Coordinate-Adjective Commas: 'A Small, Red Ball'

coordination-vs-subordination-two-ways-t.context_blurb:
There are two ways to put two ideas into one sentence. Coordination treats them as equals and joins them with one of the FANBOYS conjunctions: for, and, nor, but, or, yet and so. Subordination makes one idea lean on the other, using a subordinator such as because, although, when, since, if and while.

The choice is not decoration. Coordination says the two facts matter the same amount. Subordination says one of them is the main point and the other is the cause or the setting. So 'the rain stopped, and the game continued' reports two equal events, while 'when the rain stopped, the game continued' turns the rain into a circumstance and the game into the news.

Example: take two facts, 'She loves history' and 'It is her best subject.' Coordinated, that becomes 'She loves history, and it is her best subject.' Subordinated, it becomes 'She loves history because it is her best subject', which also repairs a run-on and tells the reader which fact is in charge.
coordination-vs-subordination-two-ways-t.title: Coordination vs Subordination: Two Ways to Combine Ideas

dangling-modifiers-walking-down-the-stre.context_blurb:
An opening phrase like 'walking down the street' has no subject of its own, so it grabs the first noun in the main clause. If that noun is the wrong one, the phrase dangles and the sentence says something absurd.

'Walking down the street, the trees were beautiful' hands the walking over to the trees. 'Rushing to catch the train, my hat blew off' puts a hat in a hurry. 'Having finished the homework, the television went on' gives the television an assignment to do. The repair never changes: make sure the noun straight after the comma is the one performing the action in the opening phrase. Either name the real doer, or give the opening phrase a subject of its own.

Example: 'While eating dinner, the dog barked' claims the dog had dinner. Name the eater and it comes right: 'While we were eating dinner, the dog barked.' Read the opening phrase, look at the very next noun, and ask whether that noun could really do it.
dangling-modifiers-walking-down-the-stre.title: Dangling Modifiers: Walking Down the Street, the Trees Were Beautiful

data-media-agenda-latin-plurals-meeting-.context_blurb:
A handful of English words arrived from Latin with their plurals attached, and English has been digesting them ever since. Datum and data, medium and media, criterion and criteria, phenomenon and phenomena all share one pattern: the singular ends in -um or -on, and the plural ends in -a.

Two of them have changed sides. Data now works as a mass noun in most modern style guides, the way water or information does, so 'the data is clear' is accepted while 'the data are clear' survives in scientific writing. Agenda began as a Latin plural meaning things to be done and is now simply singular in English, with an English plural of its own, agendas. The others still hold. One criterion, several criteria. One phenomenon, several phenomena. Stadiums has largely pushed the older Latin plural out of use.

Example: 'Only one criterion was met, but every phenomenon on the list was recorded' puts one singular against one plural, and each noun keeps its own ending.
data-media-agenda-latin-plurals-meeting-.title: Data, Media, Agenda: Latin Plurals Meeting Modern Usage

dead-metaphors-and-cliches-think-outside.context_blurb:
A cliche is a phrase that was once sharp and has been repeated until the edge wore off. It still carries its meaning, but it no longer makes a reader see anything, which is why a meeting full of thinking outside the box and moving the needle feels like wallpaper.

A dead metaphor is a different thing. It was a figure of speech once, and the figure has faded so completely that nobody notices it. The foot of a bed, the mouth of a river, the hands of a clock: none of those makes you picture a body part, and none of them is a mistake. Dead metaphors are ordinary vocabulary. George Orwell made the point in his 1946 essay 'Politics and the English Language', warning writers off any figure of speech they were used to meeting in print.

Example: 'We need to touch base and circle back' gives a reader nothing to picture, so both phrases are cliches. 'The legs of the table wobbled' is a dead metaphor doing honest work.
dead-metaphors-and-cliches-think-outside.title: Dead Metaphors and Cliches: Think Outside the Box

different-from-different-than-different-.context_blurb:
All three forms are in real use, and the difference is regional and formal rather than right against wrong.

Different from is the safe choice everywhere. It is standard in formal American writing, standard in British writing, and no editor on either side of the Atlantic will query it. Different than is common in American speech, especially in front of a clause, as when something turns out different than you had hoped. Different to is ordinary British usage and sounds foreign to an American ear. So the practical rule is short: in a school essay or any formal piece, write from. Keep than for casual American speech, and recognise to as a British habit rather than an error.

Example: 'This year's team is different from last year's' is safe in any register. 'The movie was different than the book' passes in conversation and may get marked in an essay. 'Cricket is different to baseball' tells you where the writer learned English.
different-from-different-than-different-.title: Different From, Different Than, Different to

discreet-vs-discrete-careful-vs-separate.context_blurb:
Discreet means careful, tactful, quiet about something. Discrete means separate, individual, countable as distinct units. The two words sound identical, so the spelling is the only thing that tells them apart.

The hook is in the letters. In discreet the two Es sit side by side, tucked away together, which is what a discreet person does with a secret. In discrete the T shoves the Es apart, which is what separate things are. Discrete is the one you meet in maths and science class. A discrete variable counts whole items, such as the pupils in a room, and it stands against a continuous variable like height, which flows along without gaps.

Example: 'He gave a discreet cough to warn her, then sorted the coins into three discrete piles.' The cough was quiet and tactful; the piles were separate and countable. Ask whether the sentence means tactful or means separate, and let the answer pick the spelling.
discreet-vs-discrete-careful-vs-separate.title: Discreet vs Discrete — Careful vs Separate

each-and-every-always-singular-no-matter.context_blurb:
Each and every are distributive words: they pick out one member of a group at a time. That is why both take a singular verb, no matter how many plural nouns pile up behind them.

Each of the students has a book. The plural students sits between the subject and the verb and changes nothing, because the subject is each. Every forces the singular even onto a compound subject, so every boy and girl was home by seven. The phrase 'every one of the answers' works the same way and stays singular too. One reversal is worth watching. When each comes after a plural subject instead of in front of it, the plural is in charge, so 'The students each have a book' is correct: the subject is students, and each is just trailing along behind.

Example: 'Each of the twelve players carries his own bag.' One verb and one pronoun, both singular, with twelve players standing right there in the sentence.
each-and-every-always-singular-no-matter.title: Each and Every: Always Singular, No Matter What Follows

either-and-neither-singular-as-subjects-.context_blurb:
Either and neither are singular when one of them is the subject on its own. Either of the answers is correct. Neither of the twins was home. The of-phrase behind the subject looks plural and changes nothing, exactly as it fails to change anything after each.

The picture shifts when either and neither pair up with or and nor to join two subjects. Then the verb follows whichever subject stands nearer to it. Either the cat or the dogs are outside, because dogs is nearer. Neither the dogs nor the cat is outside, because cat is nearer. That rule can produce a sentence which is correct and still grates, and the usual cure is to rearrange rather than to break the rule.

Example: 'Neither my cousins nor my aunt is driving' obeys the rule and sounds odd. 'Neither my aunt nor my cousins are driving' obeys the same rule and sounds natural, because the plural now sits beside the verb.
either-and-neither-singular-as-subjects-.title: Either and Neither: Singular As Subjects, Agreement with Correlatives

ellipsis-three-dots-vs-four.context_blurb:
Three dots mark something missing. In dialogue an ellipsis shows a voice trailing away. In a quotation it shows words that you left out.

The fourth dot is where people slip. If your omission runs to the end of a sentence, you need the three dots plus the full stop that closes that sentence, which is why four in a row is sometimes right. Three dots means words are gone from inside a sentence; four means a whole sentence ended in there as well. House styles differ on spacing, and neither version is an error. Chicago sets the dots with spaces between them, while Associated Press runs them together. Square brackets around an ellipsis tell a reader that an editor cut the words, not the original writer.

Example: a character who says 'I only meant that...' is fading out, and a character who says 'I only meant that -- ' has been cut off by somebody else. The dots soften; the dash interrupts.
ellipsis-three-dots-vs-four.title: Ellipsis: Three Dots vs Four

em-dash-the-parenthetical-break.context_blurb:
An em dash is the long one, named for the width of a capital M in the old printer's type case. Its main job is to open and close a parenthetical break in a sentence.

Three marks can do that same job, and they differ in volume. Commas are quiet and keep the aside inside the flow of the sentence. Parentheses are softer still, almost a whisper, telling a reader that the material is optional. Dashes are the loudest, interrupting the sentence and pulling the eye to whatever sits between them. A single dash also marks a thought that breaks off, and a dash in front of a name beneath a quotation credits the speaker. House styles disagree about spacing. Chicago closes the dash up tight against the words on either side, while Associated Press puts a space on each side. Either is fine, so long as you do it the same way throughout.

Example: 'The plan -- which had taken months -- finally worked' uses dashes to shout. Commas would murmur the same aside, and parentheses would bury it.
em-dash-the-parenthetical-break.title: Em-Dash: The Parenthetical Break

en-dash-for-ranges-pages-dates-scores.context_blurb:
English uses three horizontal marks of different lengths, and each one has its own job. The hyphen is shortest and glues words together: a well-written novel, a ten-year-old boy. The en dash is middle-sized, as wide as a capital N, and it means through or between. The em dash is longest and breaks a sentence open.

The en dash covers ranges of every kind: pages 34 to 37, the years 1914 to 1918, a score of three to two, a vote of nine to four. It also links two equal named things, which is why a flight route between two cities takes one instead of a hyphen.

Example: a span of years such as 1914-1918 takes an en dash, because the numbers are a range, while a war-weary country takes a hyphen, because the words are glued into one modifier. If the mark means through or between, reach for the longer one; if it is building a single word, reach for the shortest.
en-dash-for-ranges-pages-dates-scores.title: En-Dash: For Ranges (Pages, Dates, Scores)

end-punctuation-with-parenthetical-citat.context_blurb:
A parenthetical citation belongs to the sentence, not to the quotation, so the sentence's period waits until the citation is done. Write the quotation, close the quotation mark, add the citation in brackets, and only then put the full stop.

The styles differ inside the brackets. Modern Language Association style gives the author and a page number with nothing between them. American Psychological Association style gives the author and the year, separated by a comma. Chicago's author-date style gives author and year with no comma, then a comma before the page number. Block quotations reverse the order, because a block has already closed with its own period. There the citation sits outside that final stop.

Example: 'She wrote that punctuation changes everything (Truss 12).' The quoted sentence had a period of its own and it goes; the one full stop left belongs to the whole sentence, and it waits until the bracket has closed.
end-punctuation-with-parenthetical-citat.title: End Punctuation with Parenthetical Citations

ensure-insure-assure-three-verbs-three-t.context_blurb:
Three verbs sound alike and point at three different targets. You assure a person, which means you take away his doubt. You ensure an outcome, which means you make it certain. You insure property, which means you buy a policy on it.

The spellings carry the hint. Assure begins with the double S of reassure, and both are things you do to somebody. Ensure starts with the E of end result. Insure shares its opening letters with insurance. British English muddies one corner. What Americans buy as life insurance is often sold in Britain as life assurance, so that phrase is not a mistake on the other side of the Atlantic.

Example: 'I assure you the shop insures every parcel, so a signature will ensure delivery.' Three verbs, three targets: a worried person, a valuable object, and a result somebody wants guaranteed. Work out which of the three the sentence is aiming at before you choose the spelling.
ensure-insure-assure-three-verbs-three-t.title: Ensure, Insure, Assure — Three Verbs, Three Targets

eponyms-sandwiches-boycotts-and-silhouet.context_blurb:
An eponym is an ordinary word built out of a real person's name. The names fade and the words stay, which is why most people use them without ever knowing whose they were.

John Montagu, the fourth Earl of Sandwich, is said to have ordered meat between two slices of bread so that he need not leave the gaming table. Captain Charles Boycott was the English land agent whose Irish neighbours refused to deal with him in 1880, and his surname became the verb for that kind of organised refusal. Etienne de Silhouette, a French finance minister known for cheapness, lent his name to cut-paper portraits because they cost almost nothing. James Brudenell, the seventh Earl of Cardigan, wore a knitted waistcoat through the Crimean War. Franz Mesmer claimed to cure patients by animal magnetism, and the verb for holding somebody spellbound still carries his name.

Example: nicotine comes from Jean Nicot, the French ambassador who sent tobacco seeds home to Paris in 1560, so the chemical is named after a diplomat rather than after the plant.
eponyms-sandwiches-boycotts-and-silhouet.title: Eponyms: Sandwiches, Boycotts, and Silhouettes

exclamation-points-use-sparingly-one-at-.context_blurb:
An exclamation point ends a shout, a command or a burst of feeling. One is plenty. Stacking three of them signals informality at best, and at worst a writer trying to borrow excitement the sentence has not earned, so formal writing uses a single mark or none at all.

Novelists are the strictest about this. Elmore Leonard allowed himself two or three in a hundred thousand words. F. Scott Fitzgerald is supposed to have compared an exclamation point to laughing at your own joke, which is a fair description of what it does to a line that was not funny. Placement follows the speech. If the shout belongs to the quoted words, the mark goes inside the closing quotation mark.

Example: 'She shouted, "Stop!"' keeps the mark inside, because she is the one shouting. The combined mark '?!' is called an interrobang and carries a question asked in disbelief; it belongs in comics and chat, never in an essay.
exclamation-points-use-sparingly-one-at-.title: Exclamation Points: Use Sparingly, One at a Time

false-friends-eventually-and-eventualmen.context_blurb:
A false friend is a word that looks borrowed and is not. Two languages hold words that resemble each other closely, and the meanings either drifted apart or were never the same.

English eventually means at last, after some delay. Spanish eventualmente means possibly or now and then, which is almost the opposite sort of claim. Spanish actualmente and French actuellement look like actually and mean currently. German Gift looks like a present and means poison. Spanish embarazada looks like embarrassed and means pregnant, which is the mistake every beginner makes exactly once. A true cognate really does share the meaning, and a partial cognate overlaps only in part, the way French chef can mean the boss of anything while English chef has narrowed down to the kitchen.

Example: a Spanish speaker reading 'the paper will eventually be published' may hear it as 'possibly published', which is a very different promise. Same letters, different language, different meaning, so check rather than guess.
false-friends-eventually-and-eventualmen.title: False Friends: Eventually and Eventualmente

fanboys-the-seven-coordinating-conjuncti.context_blurb:
FANBOYS is a memory trick for the seven coordinating conjunctions: for, and, nor, but, or, yet and so. Coordinating means they join things of equal rank, which can be two words, two phrases or two whole sentences.

Each one carries a relationship. And adds. But and yet mark contrast. Or offers a choice, and nor offers a negative one. For and so both point at cause, with for giving the reason afterwards and so giving the result. What decides the punctuation is what sits on either side. If both sides are complete clauses, each able to stand alone as a sentence, a comma goes in front of the conjunction. If one side is only a word or a phrase, no comma is needed, which is why nobody punctuates a plain pair of nouns.

Example: 'She likes coffee and tea' joins two objects, so it takes no comma. 'She likes coffee, and her brother drinks tea' joins two clauses, so the comma goes in.
fanboys-the-seven-coordinating-conjuncti.title: FANBOYS: The Seven Coordinating Conjunctions

farther-vs-further-distance-vs-metaphor.context_blurb:
Farther is for distance you could measure with a map or a tape. Further is for everything else: more of something, an extra step, a deeper look. The hook hides in the spelling, because farther has far inside it, and far is about ground you can cross.

A handful of phrases are frozen with further and never take the other form: furthermore, without further ado, no further comment, further education. In everyday speech most people now say further for both jobs, and British English barely keeps the split at all. Careful editors and formal essays still hold the traditional line, though, so in an essay keep farther for miles and further for ideas.

Example: 'The hikers walked three miles farther before they discussed the plan any further.' The first word measures trail; the second measures talk. If a tape measure could settle it, write farther.

Swap them and a breakup turns into a road trip: 'We can't take this relationship any farther' sounds as if the car ran out of gas.
farther-vs-further-distance-vs-metaphor.title: Farther vs Further: Distance vs Metaphor

for-all-intensive-purposes-the-eggcorn-t.context_blurb:
An eggcorn is a mishearing that sticks, because the wrong version still almost makes sense. Somebody hears a phrase he has never seen in print, reaches for familiar words that sound close, and the new version starts spreading.

Several of the commonest sayings are eggcorns. The idiom underneath 'for all intensive purposes' is 'for all intents and purposes'. 'Nip it in the butt' should be 'nip it in the bud', about snipping a flower bud off before it opens. 'You have another thing coming' began as a joke about having another think coming. 'Flush out an idea' should be 'flesh out', which is what you do to a bare skeleton. And 'I could care less' says the opposite of what the speaker means, since the original claims his caring has already reached zero.

Example: the word eggcorn itself comes from somebody writing eggcorn in place of acorn. An acorn is egg-shaped and grows into a tree, so the mistake has a logic of its own, and that logic is exactly what keeps an eggcorn alive.
for-all-intensive-purposes-the-eggcorn-t.title: For All Intensive Purposes — The Eggcorn That Changes the Phrase

garden-path-sentences-the-horse-raced-pa.context_blurb:
A garden-path sentence is grammatical and still breaks your brain. It opens in a way that invites one reading, you commit to that reading, and the last word proves you wrong, so you have to go back and rebuild the sentence from the start.

The famous one is 'The horse raced past the barn fell.' Your ear takes raced as the main verb, and it is not. The horse that was raced past the barn is the one that fell, and English lets a writer drop the words 'that was', which is where the trap opens. The same trick drives 'The old man the boat', where man is a verb meaning to crew something, and 'The complex houses married soldiers', where complex is a building and houses is what it does to people. English leans on word order to signal who is doing what, so a reader guesses early and pays late. Thomas Bever brought the horse example to wide attention in 1970.

Example: 'The florist sent the flowers was pleased.' Sent looks like the main verb, but the florist who was sent the flowers is the one who was pleased.
garden-path-sentences-the-horse-raced-pa.title: Garden-Path Sentences: The Horse Raced Past the Barn Fell

historic-vs-historical-important-vs-from.context_blurb:
Historic means important enough to make history. Historical means simply belonging to the past, with no claim about importance at all. A historic battle changed something; a historical battle is just one that happened.

The pair works like a filter. Every historic event is historical, and almost nothing historical is historic. A historical novel is set in the past and may be entirely invented. A historical society studies old things. A historic building is one where something that mattered took place. Older writers sometimes put 'an historic', because they dropped the H in speech. Modern American style treats that H as sounded, so 'a historic' is standard now and the older form is fading without ever having been wrong.

Example: 'The museum keeps historical records of the town, including the deed to the historic courthouse where the trial was held.' The records are merely old; the courthouse is famous for something. Ask whether the sentence claims importance or only claims age.
historic-vs-historical-important-vs-from.title: Historic vs Historical — Important vs From-the-Past

hyphens-in-compound-modifiers-well-writt.context_blurb:
A hyphen glues two or more words into a single modifier when they sit in front of the noun they describe. A well-written novel takes the hyphen; a novel that was well written does not, because the words have moved behind the noun and no longer need gluing.

Two refinements matter. An adverb ending in -ly never takes the hyphen, so a beautifully written novel stays open. And a whole phrase can be hyphenated all the way through, which is why a boy of five becomes a five-year-old boy with a pair of hyphens. The mark is not decoration; it decides the meaning. Drop it and a man-eating shark turns into a man who is eating a shark, and a small-business owner turns into an owner who happens to be short. Chicago removes most prefix hyphens but keeps one where two words would otherwise collide, since to re-cover a couch is not to recover from flu.

Example: 'a chocolate-covered strawberry' describes the strawberry. Take the hyphen out and the words drift apart, leaving a chocolate that is covered in strawberry.
hyphens-in-compound-modifiers-well-writt.title: Hyphens in Compound Modifiers ('Well-Written Novel')

i-before-e-except-after-c-the-rule-and-i.context_blurb:
The rhyme runs: I before E, except after C, or when sounded as A, as in neighbor and weigh. It covers two cases. After a C the vowels flip, which is why receive, deceive and ceiling all put the E first. And when the pair makes an A sound it flips as well, which gives eight, weigh, sleigh and vein. Everywhere else the rhyme holds, as in believe, piece, field and chief.

Be honest about the exceptions, because there are a great many. Foreign, weird, seize, protein, caffeine and height all put E before I with no C in front and no A sound to excuse them. Science words in particular were never covered by the rhyme at all. Use it on the common everyday words, then learn the stragglers one at a time.

Example: friend keeps I before E, while neither puts E before I, and no rule on earth will tell you which is which. English spelling comes down to memory sooner or later.
i-before-e-except-after-c-the-rule-and-i.title: I Before E Except After C — The Rule and Its Exceptions

i-e-vs-e-g-that-is-vs-for-example.context_blurb:
These two Latin abbreviations are not interchangeable. The first, from id est, means 'that is', and it introduces a restatement: what follows is the same thing said again in different words. The second, from exempli gratia, means 'for the sake of example', and it introduces a sample out of a longer list.

Two hooks work. Read the first as 'in essence', because what follows is the essence of what came before. Read the second as 'example given'. If the words after the abbreviation could replace the words in front of it, you want the restatement one. If they are only some of the possibilities, you want the other. American style puts a period after each letter and a comma after the pair.

Example: 'He plays one racket sport, i.e., squash' says squash is the only one. 'He plays racket sports, e.g., squash and badminton' says those two are samples and there may well be more. Swapping them quietly shrinks a list into a definition.
i-e-vs-e-g-that-is-vs-for-example.title: I.e. vs E.g. — 'That Is' vs 'For Example'

i-vs-me-in-compound-subjects-and-objects.context_blurb:
I is a subject and me is an object. The trouble only ever shows up when the pronoun shares its slot with somebody else, because the extra name muffles your ear.

The drop test fixes every case. Take the other person out of the sentence and listen to what is left. 'Sarah and me went to the store' becomes 'me went to the store', which nobody says, so the subject form belongs there. 'The teacher gave the awards to Sarah and I' becomes 'to I', which nobody says either, so the object form belongs there instead. Watch for the overcorrection, which is the same mistake running the other way. People who have been scolded for saying me start reaching for I everywhere, including after prepositions, where it has no business.

Example: 'She invited my brother and ___.' Drop the brother and the sentence reads 'she invited me'. One mental deletion settles the whole question, every single time.
i-vs-me-in-compound-subjects-and-objects.title: I vs Me in Compound Subjects and Objects

if-i-was-vs-if-i-were-the-subjunctive-mo.context_blurb:
Were in an if-clause marks something contrary to fact. Was in an if-clause marks something that may really have happened. The choice tells a reader which kind of claim is being made.

'If I were you' takes were, because I am not you and never will be. 'If I was rude yesterday, I apologise' takes was, because the rudeness may be a real event; the sentence means 'if it is true that I was rude'. The same split runs through wishes, which are contrary to fact by definition, so a wish always takes were. For a hypothesis about the past, the verb steps back one further and takes had, so a thing that did not happen gets 'had known' rather than 'knew'.

Example: 'If the dog were mine, I would walk him every morning' tells you the dog belongs to somebody else. Swap were for was and the sentence turns into a question about who owns the animal. Ask whether the if-clause is impossible or merely uncertain.
if-i-was-vs-if-i-were-the-subjunctive-mo.title: If I Was vs If I Were: The Subjunctive Mood

imply-vs-infer-speaker-vs-listener.context_blurb:
Imply and infer sit at opposite ends of the same message. A speaker implies, hinting at something without saying it outright. A listener infers, drawing a conclusion from what he just heard. One sends; the other receives.

The hook is the opening letters. Imply belongs to the person putting the hint In. Infer belongs to the person taking it In. So a tone of voice implies that a test is coming, and the pupils infer that they had better revise. The common error runs one way. Somebody accuses another person of inferring when he means implying. Writers have muddled the two since the sixteenth century, and modern style guides still ask you to hold them apart, because the distinction earns its keep.

Example: 'His shrug implied that he did not believe her, and she inferred the rest.' He produced the hint and she worked it out. If the sentence is about the one who spoke, use the first verb; if it is about the one listening, use the second.
imply-vs-infer-speaker-vs-listener.title: Imply vs Infer — Speaker vs Listener

indefinite-pronouns-everyone-each-either.context_blurb:
Indefinite pronouns point at people or things without naming them: everyone, everybody, someone, anyone, nobody, each, either, neither. Nearly all of them are singular, and they take a singular verb even when a plural noun is standing right beside them.

Everyone is welcome. Each of the students has a book. Neither of the answers is correct. In every one of those, the plural word sits inside a prepositional phrase and cannot reach the verb. Cross the phrase out with your finger and the right form is obvious. None is the one that genuinely flexes. It takes its number from whatever it refers to, so 'none of the milk is left' and 'none of the cookies are left' are both defensible, and most editors allow either.

Example: 'Somebody has left his coat on the bus.' Somebody is one person, so the verb and the pronoun both stay singular, however many passengers were riding along.
indefinite-pronouns-everyone-each-either.title: Indefinite Pronouns: Everyone, Each, Either Take Singular Verbs

independent-vs-dependent-clauses-the-sta.context_blurb:
A clause is any group of words with a subject and a verb. Whether it can stand on its own is what splits the two kinds apart.

An independent clause is already a whole sentence: 'She laughed.' A dependent clause has a subject and a verb too, but it opens with a word that makes it lean on something else: 'Because she laughed.' Those leaning words are subordinators, and the list is short enough to learn by heart: because, although, since, while, if, when, until, unless, after and before. The standalone test is the entire skill. Put a full stop at the end of the clause and read it aloud. If it sounds finished, the clause is independent. If it leaves you waiting, the clause is dependent, and a dependent clause left by itself is a fragment.

Example: 'Although the bus was late, we got to school on time.' The second half passes the test and the first half fails it, which is exactly why the first half needs the second one to finish it off.
independent-vs-dependent-clauses-the-sta.title: Independent vs Dependent Clauses: The Standalone Test

intentional-fragments-when-writers-break.context_blurb:
A fragment is a group of words punctuated as a sentence without being one. Usually that is an accident: a dropped verb, or a subordinate clause left standing on its own. Sometimes it is a deliberate choice.

A deliberate fragment is short, lands hard, and follows a complete sentence that has already set the scene, so a reader never loses the thread. 'It was cold. Bitterly cold.' Nothing is actually missing there, because the first sentence supplied everything the second one needs. That is the test for telling style from error: ask whether a reader can finish the fragment out of the sentence before it. Formal writing keeps away from the device. A school essay, a lab report or a legal letter wants complete sentences throughout, so a fragment there reads as carelessness rather than punch.

Example: 'The door opened. Slowly.' works in a story and would be marked in a science write-up, where it should simply say that the door opened slowly.
intentional-fragments-when-writers-break.title: Intentional Fragments: When Writers Break the Rule on Purpose

introductory-phrase-commas-after-dinner-.context_blurb:
An introductory word, phrase or clause takes a comma to show a reader where it ends and the main sentence begins. After dinner, we walked the dog. When the storm passed, the game restarted. Well, that was odd.

Flip the order and the comma disappears, because nothing is being introduced any more: we walked the dog after dinner. Chicago also lets you leave the comma out when the opener is very short and cannot be misread, so 'In 1776 the colonies declared independence' passes as it stands. The comma stops being optional the moment a sentence could be misread without it, and that is the real reason behind the rule.

Example: 'While eating the cat watched television' invites a horrible first reading, because the eye takes the cat as the thing being eaten. One comma after eating puts the cat back at the table instead of on the menu. Read your opener aloud and listen for where the pause falls.
introductory-phrase-commas-after-dinner-.title: Introductory-Phrase Commas: 'After Dinner, We Went Out'

ironic-not-unfortunate-and-not-coinciden.context_blurb:
Irony needs a reversal. Something happens that is the opposite of what the setup led everybody to expect, and the gap between the two is where the irony lives. Bad luck is not irony. A coincidence is not irony either.

Three kinds are worth naming. Verbal irony says the opposite of what is meant, which is the machinery inside sarcasm. Situational irony reverses an outcome, so the thing designed to prevent a disaster is the thing that causes one. Dramatic irony is the kind a theatre audience enjoys, where the watchers know something the character on stage does not, which is why Oedipus hunting the murderer of King Laius is the standard example.

Example: rain on a wedding day is simply unfortunate, because nothing about a wedding ever promised sunshine. A plumber coming home to a burst pipe is ironic, because his whole trade is the promise that this will not happen. Test any candidate by asking what was expected and whether the result turned that expectation inside out.
ironic-not-unfortunate-and-not-coinciden.title: Ironic: Not 'Unfortunate' and Not 'Coincidental'

irregardless-the-double-negative-that-is.context_blurb:
Regardless already means without regard to something, and the ending -less is what does the negating. Bolt ir- onto the front, which is itself a negative in irrational, irrelevant and irregular, and you get a word that negates twice and adds nothing at all.

That is why style guides warn against it and why dictionaries label it nonstandard. Nonstandard is not the same as nonexistent: people really do say it, and recording the words people say is what a dictionary is for. When Merriam-Webster drew attention to its entry in 2020, the editors pointed out that listing a word reports usage rather than approving of it. Two words do the job properly. Regardless is the plain one. Irrespective is the formal one, and it means without respect to.

Example: write 'regardless of the cost, the plan goes ahead', or 'irrespective of the cost, the plan goes ahead'. Both are standard English, and neither one says not twice over.
irregardless-the-double-negative-that-is.title: Irregardless — The Double-Negative That Isn't a Word (Mostly)

italics-vs-quotation-marks-for-titles.context_blurb:
The rule is about size, not importance. A whole, free-standing work goes in italics. A part of a larger work goes in quotation marks.

So a book, a film, a newspaper, an album, a play and a television series all take italics. A chapter, a short poem, an article, a song and a single episode all take quotation marks, because each of those lives inside something bigger. The two often appear side by side, with the series in italics and the episode in quotation marks right after it. Italics do two other jobs as well. A foreign word that English has not yet absorbed takes italics on its first appearance. And the name of one individual ship, train or spacecraft is italicised, while the name of a whole class of them is not.

Example: a song title sits inside quotation marks and the album it came from goes in italics, so a reader can see at a glance which of the two contains the other.
italics-vs-quotation-marks-for-titles.title: Italics vs Quotation Marks for Titles

its-vs-its-the-apostrophe-that-flips-mea.context_blurb:
One apostrophe decides which of two words you wrote. It's, with the mark, is always a squashed it is or it has, and the apostrophe stands where the letters went missing. Its, with no mark, is the possessive. It stays bare for the same reason his, hers, ours and theirs do: a personal pronoun never uses an apostrophe to own something. A team, a band or a country is one thing, so it owns with the bare form too.

Two tests settle every case. Read it is or it has in place of the word; if the sentence survives, keep the apostrophe. Or try his in the slot; if his fits, leave the mark off.

Example: 'It's been raining all week, and the garden has lost its tomatoes.' It has been survives the swap, so the first word takes the mark. His tomatoes fits the second slot, so that one stays bare.

Get it wrong and a pet turns into a riddle: 'The parrot ate it's dinner' claims the parrot ate it is dinner.
its-vs-its-the-apostrophe-that-flips-mea.title: Its vs It's: The Apostrophe That Flips Meaning

less-vs-fewer-mass-vs-count.context_blurb:
Fewer counts things one at a time; less measures stuff you cannot count. A count noun has a plural and takes a number in front of it: three books, ten people. A mass noun gets measured instead: water, advice, homework. Count nouns take fewer, and mass nouns take less. The quick check is to put the number two in front of the noun. If it sounds normal, you want fewer.

Measurements break the pattern on purpose. Time, weight, money and distance behave as one amount even though the unit has a plural, so a film runs less than two hours and a bag weighs less than five kilos. Most usage guides treat a percentage the same way, as a proportion rather than a pile, so less is the usual choice there too.

Example: 'The bakery sold fewer muffins this week, so it used less flour.' Muffins can be counted; flour is measured.

Mix them up and the school newsletter boasts that there are 'less bullies this year', as if the bullies had all gone on a diet.
less-vs-fewer-mass-vs-count.title: Less vs Fewer — Mass vs Count

literally-the-strict-meaning-vs-the-inte.context_blurb:
Literally means the words are to be taken at face value, with no exaggeration and no figure of speech. If a pot literally boiled over, there is water on the stove.

Used loosely it becomes an intensifier meaning very, and the sentence then claims something impossible. A person who literally exploded with laughter would be spread across the room, and that is where the eye-rolling comes from. Be fair about the history, though. The loose use is not a modern invention; novelists were doing it in the early nineteenth century, Charlotte Bronte and Charles Dickens among them. So it is standard informal English rather than an illiterate blunder. Formal writing is where you hold the line. In a lab report, an essay or a news story, keep the word for things that are true word for word, and cut it everywhere else.

Example: 'The thermometer literally hit forty degrees' is a measurement. 'I literally died' is a figure of speech, and the strict reading would call for a funeral.
literally-the-strict-meaning-vs-the-inte.title: Literally: The Strict Meaning vs the Intensifier

lose-vs-loose-one-o-or-two.context_blurb:
Lose is a verb: to misplace something, or to fail to win. Loose is usually an adjective: not tight, not fastened, free to move about. The difference on the page is one letter, and the difference in sound is real, since lose rhymes with news while loose rhymes with goose.

The hook is the spare O. Loose has two of them, spread out, which is what loose things are. Lose has only one, because you end up with less than you started with. Loose works as a verb as well, meaning to set free, as when an archer looses an arrow, but that use is rare enough that the adjective can be your default.

Example: 'If the strap is loose, you will lose the bag.' One word describes the strap and the other says what happens next. The noun built from the verb is loss, which keeps the single O and swaps the ending.
lose-vs-loose-one-o-or-two.title: Lose vs Loose — One O or Two

malapropism-mrs-malaprop-and-the-wrong-w.context_blurb:
A malapropism is the wrong word in the right slot, close enough in sound to be funny. The name comes from Mrs Malaprop in Richard Brinsley Sheridan's 1775 play 'The Rivals', who calls a man the pineapple of politeness when she means the pinnacle, and who describes a woman as headstrong as an allegory on the banks of the Nile when she means an alligator. Sheridan built the name out of the French phrase mal a propos, which means badly suited to the occasion.

Two cousins get confused with it. A spoonerism swaps the opening sounds of nearby words, so a well-oiled bicycle turns into a well-boiled icicle. An eggcorn is a misheard phrase rebuilt out of words that still sort of fit, the way intents and purposes turns into intensive purposes.

Example: Yogi Berra reporting that Texas has a lot of electrical votes is a malapropism, since electoral was the word he was reaching for and the two sound nearly alike.
malapropism-mrs-malaprop-and-the-wrong-w.title: Malapropism: Mrs. Malaprop and the Wrong Word for the Right Sound

may-vs-might-permission-and-possibility.context_blurb:
May does two jobs: it asks for or grants permission, and it reports a real possibility. Might reports possibility too, but a fainter one. Snow in December may happen; snow in July might happen.

Because may carries both jobs, it can produce a genuinely ambiguous sentence. 'You may not go to the party' either refuses permission or predicts that you probably will not get there, and only the situation decides which reading is live. Might is historically the past form of may, which is why it takes over in reported speech and in any hypothesis about something that did not happen. A missed train is always a might: if we had hurried, we might have caught it. Using may there would hint that the train is still an option.

Example: 'May I leave the table?' asks a parent for permission. 'I might leave early' reports a plan that could still change. Ask whether the sentence wants permission, a likely outcome or a long shot.
may-vs-might-permission-and-possibility.title: May vs Might: Permission and Possibility

measurements-and-amounts-two-hundred-mil.context_blurb:
