A plural-looking amount takes a singular verb when the whole amount counts as one thing. Two hundred miles is a long drive, because the distance is a single stretch of road rather than two hundred separate miles. Ten dollars is the price, three hours is the wait, two gallons is what remains in the tank.

The verb turns plural the moment the units are genuinely being counted one by one. Ten dollar bills were scattered across the floor, because each note is a separate object somebody could pick up. That is the question to put to the sentence: is the number working as one measurement, or as a collection of individual items?

Example: 'Fifteen minutes is enough time to walk there' measures one stretch of the afternoon. 'The fifteen minutes before a test are the worst' counts them out one after another, so the verb follows the items instead of the amount.
measurements-and-amounts-two-hundred-mil.title: Measurements and Amounts: 'Two Hundred Miles IS a Long Drive'

metaphor-vs-simile-with-or-without-like-.context_blurb:
A simile compares two things and admits it, using like or as. A metaphor makes the claim flat out, saying that one thing is the other. That single word is the whole difference, which is why so many famous similes get called metaphors by mistake.

Robert Burns writing that his love is like a red, red rose has written a simile, because the word like is sitting right there in the line. Shakespeare writing that all the world's a stage has written a metaphor, and because he carries the same comparison on through acts, exits and the ages of a life, it counts as an extended metaphor. An analogy is the next step out. It maps the parts of something unfamiliar onto the parts of something familiar, which is what a teacher does by lining an atom up against a solar system.

Example: 'He fought like a lion' is a simile, and 'he was a lion in the field' is a metaphor. Look for like or as before you name the figure.
metaphor-vs-simile-with-or-without-like-.title: Metaphor vs Simile: With or Without LIKE / AS

misplaced-modifiers-i-saw-the-boy-with-t.context_blurb:
A modifier attaches itself to whatever sits nearest to it. Put it in the wrong place and the sentence still parses, but it describes the wrong thing and the reader gets a picture nobody intended.

'I saw the boy with the telescope' leaves two readings standing, because the phrase could belong to the seeing or to the boy. Move it next to the word it modifies and the sentence settles down. Small words behave the same way: 'she only eats vegetables on Tuesdays' parks only beside eats, when the writer probably meant it to sit beside Tuesdays. Almost is just as slippery, and shifting it changes how many plates survived. A misplaced modifier sits in the wrong slot. A dangling modifier has no correct slot at all, because the noun it ought to describe never turns up in the sentence.

Example: 'She served hot dogs to children in paper cups' puts the children inside the cups. Write 'she served hot dogs in paper cups to children' and the cups go back to the food.
misplaced-modifiers-i-saw-the-boy-with-t.title: Misplaced Modifiers: I Saw the Boy with the Telescope

nauseous-vs-nauseated-the-strict-distinc.context_blurb:
The strict pair splits the cause from the symptom. Something nauseous makes other people feel ill; a person who feels ill is nauseated. The endings do the work: the -ous word describes the source of the trouble, and the -ated word describes the victim of it.

That is why careful editors wince at 'I feel nauseous.' Read strictly, the speaker has announced that he is the smell, and that everybody standing near him is about to turn green. Nauseated was the word he wanted.

Be honest about where the language has gone, though. Since the middle of the twentieth century so many Americans have used the -ous word for the sick feeling that dictionaries now list both senses, and the strict split survives mainly in medical and formal writing. Learn it anyway, because an editor will hold you to it.

Example: 'The nauseous reek of the bilge left half the crew nauseated below deck.' The smell causes it, and the sailors suffer it.
nauseous-vs-nauseated-the-strict-distinc.title: Nauseous vs Nauseated: The Strict Distinction

nominalizations-zombie-nouns-that-hide-t.context_blurb:
A nominalisation is a verb wearing a noun costume. Decide becomes decision, implement becomes implementation, improve becomes improvement, fail becomes failure. The action is still in the sentence, but it has stopped happening: it sits there as an abstract lump while some limp helper (made, conducted, resulted in, was) does the grammatical work.

Watch for the endings -tion, -sion, -ment, -ence and -ance, especially when two or three of them queue up in one clause. The cure is to dig out the buried verb, give it a human subject, and let it act. Sentences usually lose a third of their words and gain a person.

Example: 'The utilisation of the library by students showed an increase after the renovation of the reading room.' Dig out the verbs and it becomes: 'More students used the library after the school renovated the reading room.' Same facts, half the fog, and now somebody is actually doing something.
nominalizations-zombie-nouns-that-hide-t.title: Nominalizations: Zombie Nouns That Hide the Verb

none-singular-or-plural-depending-on-ref.context_blurb:
None is not locked to the singular, whatever a strict schoolteacher may claim. It grew out of an Old English phrase meaning not one, and it has carried both a not-one sense and a not-any sense for more than a thousand years. So the verb follows the noun you are really talking about, plus the emphasis you want.

Two tests settle nearly every case. If the thing after of can be counted and you mean not any of them, the plural sounds right: none of the biscuits are left. If the thing after of cannot be counted, as with water, money, flour or time, the singular is forced, because a mass noun never takes a plural verb. And when you want the hard not-a-single-one thud, choose the singular on purpose.

Example: 'None of the paint was wasted, but none of the brushes were cleaned.' Paint cannot be counted, brushes can, and each verb simply obeys its own noun.
none-singular-or-plural-depending-on-ref.title: None: Singular or Plural Depending on Referent

number-majority-half-verb-depends-on-wha.context_blurb:
With a subject shaped X of Y, such as a number of, the majority of, half of, a lot of or fifty percent of, the verb usually listens to Y, the noun after of. Count nouns pull the plural; mass nouns pull the singular. Half of the pies vanish, while half of the pie vanishes.

One pair breaks that pattern, and the little word in front decides it. A number of means several, so it takes a plural verb. The number of names one quantity, a single figure that can rise or fall, so it takes a singular verb. Majority behaves the same way: as a crowd of people it goes plural, as a measured share it goes singular. Work and money cannot be counted at all, so they stay singular however much of them there is.

Example: 'A number of ducks are missing from the pond, although the number of ducks has never been high.' The first clause counts birds, the second counts one total.
number-majority-half-verb-depends-on-wha.title: Number, Majority, Half: Verb Depends on What's Being Counted

numbers-when-to-spell-out-when-to-use-di.context_blurb:
The Chicago rule is friendly to readers: write out whole numbers from zero up to a hundred, and write out round hundreds, thousands and millions too. Everything else goes in digits. News style is tighter, since the Associated Press switches to digits at ten, so check which house you are writing for before you argue.

Three rules override everything else. A sentence never opens with a numeral, so either recast the sentence or spell the number out. Spelled-out compounds from twenty-one through ninety-nine take a hyphen. American style groups long numerals with commas, so 1,000,000 rather than 1.000.000 or a bare row of zeros. Ordinals in running prose are words, not tiny raised letters.

Example: 'Twenty-seven swimmers entered, but only 112 of the 1,250 tickets sold.' The opener is spelled out because it begins the sentence, twenty-seven earns its hyphen, and the two large figures stay in digits where a reader can take them in at a glance.
numbers-when-to-spell-out-when-to-use-di.title: Numbers: When to Spell Out, When to Use Digits

onomatopoeia-words-that-sound-like-what-.context_blurb:
Onomatopoeia is the trick of spelling a noise. The word imitates the sound it names, which is why buzz, hiss, plop, crunch, moo and meow feel right the moment you say them out loud. The term comes from Greek onoma, a name, and poiein, to make: you make a name out of a noise.

Three things are worth knowing. Comic-book noises count, and bam, pow and zap all sit in ordinary dictionaries now. Some animals are named for their own cry rather than for their looks, which is why a cuckoo is called a cuckoo. And the spelling is not universal, because each language hears through its own alphabet: a dog says woof in English, wan-wan in Japanese and gav-gav in Russian. Do not confuse the trick with alliteration, which repeats the opening consonant of neighbouring words, as in Peter Piper picked a peck.

Example: 'The screen door banged, the kettle shrieked, and the cat yowled.' Three noises, three words that already contain them.
onomatopoeia-words-that-sound-like-what-.title: Onomatopoeia: Words That Sound Like What They Mean

palindromes-sentences-that-read-the-same.context_blurb:
A palindrome reads the same in both directions. Single words manage it easily, as level, kayak, noon, rotor and racecar all do, and the game only gets interesting at sentence length, where you ignore spaces, capitals and punctuation and judge the letters alone.

The famous ones are short and smug. 'Madam, I am Adam' is the oldest party trick. 'Never odd or even' and 'Step on no pets' both work. Leigh Mercer, a British wordplay fanatic, published the seven-word Panama Canal palindrome in 1948, and it is still the one everybody quotes. Beware of the Napoleon line about Elba: it is a real palindrome but a fake quotation, composed by an English puzzler in the nineteenth century, and the emperor never said it.

Keep two cousins separate. A pangram crams every letter of the alphabet into one sentence, and an anagram rearranges the letters of a phrase into something new.

Example: 'Was it a car or a cat I saw?' Spell it backwards letter by letter and the sentence comes back unchanged.
palindromes-sentences-that-read-the-same.title: Palindromes: Sentences That Read the Same Backwards

panda-punctuation-eats-shoots-and-leaves.context_blurb:
Lynne Truss put a panda on the cover of her 2003 book Eats, Shoots and Leaves, subtitled the Zero Tolerance approach to punctuation, and the joke on the cover is the whole lesson. Without commas the words are a diet: the animal eats shoots and leaves, which is exactly what a panda lives on. Add one comma after the first verb and the animal becomes a gunman who finishes lunch, fires a shot and walks out. In Truss's telling the panda hands over a badly punctuated wildlife manual on his way through the door.

Truss is a cheerful prescriptivist: she holds that there is a right way to punctuate and that a writer should be taught it rather than excused. A comma marks a break in the flow, so dropping one or adding one does not merely tidy a sentence, it reassigns the words to different jobs.

Example: 'Most of the time, travellers worry about luggage.' Drop that comma and the sentence is suddenly about time travellers, who presumably worry about other things.
panda-punctuation-eats-shoots-and-leaves.title: Panda Punctuation: 'Eats, Shoots and Leaves'

pangram-and-anagram-every-letter-or-the-.context_blurb:
Three word games are easy to mix up. A pangram packs every letter of the alphabet into one sentence, which is why typists and font designers love them, and the one about a quick brown fox and a lazy dog is the famous example. An anagram keeps the letters of a word or phrase and shuffles them into something new. A palindrome reads identically forwards and backwards.

The test for an anagram is arithmetic, not instinct: count each letter on both sides and the two tallies must match exactly. Debit card rearranges into bad credit because both hold the same nine letters. Eleven plus two rearranges into twelve plus one, which may be the finest anagram in English, since the two phrases also come to the same total. Drop a letter or borrow one and you have a near miss, not an anagram.

Example: 'Sphinx of black quartz, judge my vow.' Twenty-nine letters, and all twenty-six of the alphabet turn up at least once.
pangram-and-anagram-every-letter-or-the-.title: Pangram and Anagram: Every Letter, or the Letters Rearranged

parallel-structure-in-lists-same-grammat.context_blurb:
Parallel structure means every item in a list wears the same grammatical uniform. All gerunds, or all infinitives, or all plain nouns, or all adjectives. The ear notices the instant one item breaks ranks, even when a reader cannot name what went wrong.

Here is the test. Find the words that come before the list, then read them separately into each item. 'I like running, swimming, and to bike' gives you 'I like running', 'I like swimming' and 'I like to bike', and the third one lurches. Fix the odd item rather than adding words: biking. The same test catches a list that opens with adjectives and finishes with a whole clause, as in 'She was smart, kind, and had a good sense of humour', where the cure is one more adjective.

Example: 'The coach told us to stretch, to drink water, and resting between sets.' Read the opener into each branch, hear the last one collapse, and change it to 'to rest' so the sentence marches.
parallel-structure-in-lists-same-grammat.title: Parallel Structure in Lists: Same Grammatical Form

parallel-structure-with-correlative-conj.context_blurb:
Correlative conjunctions work in fixed pairs: either with or, neither with nor, both with and, whether with or, and the long one, not only followed by but also. Each half of the pair is a hinge, and whatever grammatical shape follows the first hinge must follow the second.

So look at the word standing immediately after each hinge. If an infinitive follows the first, an infinitive must follow the second; if a noun follows the first, a noun must follow the second. 'She either wants to visit Paris or eating in Rome' fails because an infinitive on the left meets a gerund on the right. Moving the hinge often fixes more than rewriting does, since shifting one word in front of or behind the first half can line both branches up at once.

Example: 'The dog not only chewed my homework but also the table leg.' A verb follows the first hinge and a bare noun follows the second. Repair it as 'chewed not only my homework but also the table leg.'
parallel-structure-with-correlative-conj.title: Parallel Structure with Correlative Conjunctions (Both/and, Either/or, Not Only/but Also)

parentheses-vs-brackets-aside-vs-editori.context_blurb:
Round parentheses belong to the writer. He drops in his own aside, lowers his voice for a moment, and a reader can skip it without losing the thread. Square brackets belong to whoever comes later: they mark words that an editor has pushed into somebody else's quotation, so a reader always knows which hand wrote them.

That one distinction settles the usual puzzles. Clarifying a pronoun inside a quotation takes brackets, never parentheses. Flagging a mistake you are preserving on purpose takes the Latin tag sic in brackets, straight after the error. Cutting words out of the middle of a quotation takes an ellipsis in brackets, which is how a reader tells an editor's snip from a speaker trailing off. And when one aside has to sit inside another, the inner pair switches to brackets so the pairs do not blur.

Example: 'She testified, I watched him [my brother] leave the gate open.' The quotation is hers, and the two words naming the brother are not.
parentheses-vs-brackets-aside-vs-editori.title: Parentheses vs Brackets: Aside vs Editorial Insertion

passive-voice-when-it-hides-the-actor.context_blurb:
A sentence is passive when its subject receives the action instead of doing it. Learn the shape and you will spot it anywhere: a form of to be plus a past participle, as in was broken, is boiled, were discovered. English then lets a writer drop the doer altogether, and that is where the trouble starts, because a sentence can report an event while quietly losing the person behind it.

The passive earns its keep in three situations: nobody knows who acted, everybody already knows, or the process matters more than the hand behind it. A stolen bicycle and a liquid heated in a laboratory both belong in the passive. The voice turns slippery only when a reader deserves to know who is responsible and the sentence declines to say.

Example: 'The window was smashed during practice' leaves nobody accountable. 'Dario smashed the window with a line drive' costs about the same number of words and tells a reader who owes the glazier.
passive-voice-when-it-hides-the-actor.title: Passive Voice: When It Hides the Actor

peaked-peeked-piqued-three-verbs-one-sou.context_blurb:
Three spellings, one sound, three jobs. A peak is a summit, so a mountain peaks and a fever peaks. To peek is to glance quickly, usually at something you were not invited to look at. To pique is to prick or to stir up, which is why a mystery piques your curiosity and why a sulk is called a fit of pique.

Hang each one on its own letters. The A in peak has a pointed top like a mountain. The double E in peek is a pair of eyes at a keyhole. And pique came into English from French in the 1600s, from a verb meaning to prick, so the sharp jab is sitting inside the word.

Example: 'She peeked at the summit photograph, and the climb that had peaked at fourteen thousand feet piqued her interest in going back.' One quick glance, one high point, one prod to the curiosity, and only the last of the three has anything to do with wanting something.
peaked-peeked-piqued-three-verbs-one-sou.title: Peaked, Peeked, Piqued — Three Verbs, One Sound

portmanteau-lewis-carrolls-word-suitcase.context_blurb:
A portmanteau is a word made by folding two words into one, sharing the seam where they meet. Lewis Carroll named the trick in Through the Looking-Glass, where Humpty Dumpty tells Alice that a word can be packed like a travelling case with two meanings inside. Smoke and fog give smog. Breakfast and lunch give brunch. An iPod and a broadcast gave podcast.

Keep three kinds of made-up word apart. A portmanteau overlaps and loses letters at the join. A compound bolts two whole words together, as in bookshelf, and nothing is lost. An acronym is built from the first letters of a phrase, which is where scuba came from. Carroll invented dozens of blends for Jabberwocky in 1871, and two of them escaped the poem into real dictionaries: galumphing, from gallop and triumphing, and chortle, from chuckle and snort.

Example: spoon and fork give spork. Say the two words quickly, hear where they overlap, and the seam is the whole joke.
portmanteau-lewis-carrolls-word-suitcase.title: Portmanteau: Lewis Carroll's Word-Suitcases

possessive-apostrophes-singular-plural-a.context_blurb:
An apostrophe in a possessive marks ownership, never a plural. Work in two steps: write the owner first, then add the apostrophe. One dog owns the bone, so the owner is dog and the bone is the dog's. Several dogs own the bones, so the owner is dogs and the apostrophe lands behind that s. Irregular plurals have no final s to work around, which is why the toys belong to the children.

A plain plural takes nothing at all. 'The Smith's live next door' hands the family house to an apostrophe that owns nothing, and the same error litters shop windows: 'The cat's are everywhere.'

Names already ending in s are the one genuinely disputed case. Chicago adds the full apostrophe and s, so the book belongs to James's. Newspaper style following the Associated Press gives a singular proper name the apostrophe alone. Pick a house and keep to it.

Example: 'The boys' coach borrowed Charles's whistle.' Several boys, one Charles, and not a plural in sight.
possessive-apostrophes-singular-plural-a.title: Possessive Apostrophes: Singular, Plural, and Names Ending in S

principal-vs-principle-the-person-the-mo.context_blurb:
Two spellings, three meanings, one easy hook. The -al word ends in pal, and the principal is the pal who runs the school. Stretch that same word and it means chief or most important, as in the principal reason or the principal violinist. In banking it names the lump you borrowed, the amount that interest is charged on top of. The -le word is a rule or a belief: a scientific law, or a line you refuse to cross.

So test the sentence by substitution. If main or chief fits the slot, you want the -al spelling. If rule or belief fits, you want -le. Only the -al form can be a person, and only the -le form can be a conviction, which is why a man of principle is a different creature from a principal.

Example: 'The principal cause of the leak was a cracked pipe, and the plumber fixed it on principle, free of charge.' Main cause, settled conviction, two spellings doing two jobs.
principal-vs-principle-the-person-the-mo.title: Principal vs Principle — The Person, the Money, the Rule

pronoun-agreement-his-her-or-its.context_blurb:
A pronoun has to match the number of the noun it points back to. One thing takes a singular pronoun, more than one takes a plural, and no amount of modern habit changes the arithmetic. The words that look like crowds are the trap: everyone, everybody, someone, nobody, each, either and neither are all grammatically singular, so each of them takes he, she or it.

Pick the pronoun by what the word actually names. A person whose sex is unknown traditionally takes he, him and his. A mixed group can take the paired form his or her, used sparingly, because that form clogs a sentence fast. An animal or an object takes it and its. And when the paired form starts piling up, rewrite in the plural instead: make the subject students, cats or campers, and honest plural pronouns follow.

Example: 'Each knight sits in ___ seat.' The subject is one knight at a time, so the blank takes his, and the Round Table stays orderly.
pronoun-agreement-his-her-or-its.title: Pronoun Agreement: His, Her or Its

pronoun-antecedent-agreement-matching-nu.context_blurb:
The antecedent is the noun a pronoun points back to, and the two must match in number and in person. Slip between them and a reader stumbles: open a sentence about one company and finish it with a plural pronoun, and the sentence has quietly changed subject halfway through. The same slip happens with person, when a writer starts with one and finishes with you.

Collective nouns are where this gets argued. A team, a jury, a staff, a company, a band, a family: each is one body made of many members. American usage treats the body as a single thing, so a jury reaches its verdict and a company pays its staff. British usage often goes plural when the members act separately, which is why an English newspaper writes that Liverpool are winning. If the individual members are the point, name them, and let a real plural carry the pronoun.

Example: 'The orchestra played its last concert on Friday, and the musicians packed their instruments afterwards.' One body, then many people.
pronoun-antecedent-agreement-matching-nu.title: Pronoun-Antecedent Agreement: Matching Number and Person

punctuation-and-emojis-the-modern-inform.context_blurb:
Punctuation carries tone, and in texting the tone has drifted. A full stop at the end of a one-line message now reads as cold or annoyed, because the sentence did not need the mark and the sender added it anyway. A trailing row of dots reads as reluctant or faintly pointed. Capitals all the way through read as shouting, which is why formal prose uses italics for emphasis instead. Gretchen McCulloch described this whole informal system in her 2019 book about internet language.

None of it is a licence for formal writing. Stacked marks, strings of question marks and emojis stay in the casual register, and the major style guides have no rule admitting them. Know the register you are in, and let the reader's expectations settle the mark.

Example: a friend texts 'sure' and you read it as cheerful. He texts 'Sure.' and you spend the afternoon wondering what you did wrong. Same word, one extra mark, two completely different moods.
punctuation-and-emojis-the-modern-inform.title: Punctuation and Emojis: The Modern Informal Register

punctuation-with-abbreviations-us-vs-u-s.context_blurb:
American practice puts a period after a shortened title: Dr., Mr., Mrs., Prof. Beyond that the houses disagree, and the disagreement is the lesson. Chicago now drops the periods from most capital-letter abbreviations and prints PhD and US, while the Associated Press keeps them in the country name and prints U.S. in the body of a story. Neither is wrong; they are different employers.

Two mechanical rules never change. An abbreviation that ends a sentence does not take a second dot, because one period does both jobs and a stacked pair looks like a typo. And a Latin abbreviation used mid-sentence keeps its own periods and then takes a comma before whatever it introduces, which is how e.g., and i.e., are set in American style.

Example: 'Mrs. Alvarez earned her PhD in Oslo, moved back in 1998, and still keeps a flat in the U.S.' Three abbreviations, each punctuated its own way, and only one dot at the very end.
punctuation-with-abbreviations-us-vs-u-s.title: Punctuation with Abbreviations: US vs U.S. vs USA

punctuation-with-parenthetical-asides-co.context_blurb:
Once you have chosen a mark for an aside, the punctuation inside it follows one rule: a mark belongs to whatever it finishes. A complete sentence standing on its own between parentheses keeps its period inside them. An aside tucked into a larger sentence has no period of its own, and the host sentence's full stop waits outside the closing bracket.

Two sentences get rescued this way. When one aside has to sit inside another, switch the inner pair to square brackets so a reader can see which mark closes what. And when commas are already swarming, promote the outer aside to dashes, since a sentence with five commas in it hides its own skeleton. That is the order of volume, by the way: commas speak normally, dashes shout, parentheses murmur.

Example: 'The ferry, late again, as it had been all week, reached the island at noon.' Three commas and no skeleton. Give the outer aside a pair of dashes and the sentence snaps back into shape.
punctuation-with-parenthetical-asides-co.title: Punctuation with Parenthetical Asides: Commas, Dashes, or Parens

question-marks-inside-quotes-at-the-end-.context_blurb:
The question mark belongs to a real question only. If a sentence merely reports that a question happened, it is a statement and takes a full stop: she asked where I went. Writing that as a question is the commonest slip here, because the writer hears the question inside his own sentence and punctuates the echo.

Placement with quotation marks follows ownership. If the quoted words are the question, the mark goes inside the closing quotes. If the whole sentence is a question about something quoted, the mark goes outside them. A statement with a check bolted onto the end, called a tag question, as in 'you are coming, aren't you?', ends with the mark because the tag turns the whole thing into a query. And a question about a question never doubles up: one mark, at the very end, however many questions are nested inside.

Example: 'Did he really shout stop the bus?' The shout was an order, the sentence is the question, so the mark waits outside the quoted words.
question-marks-inside-quotes-at-the-end-.title: Question Marks: Inside Quotes, at the End, in Indirect Questions

quotation-marks-american-vs-british-punc.context_blurb:
American style tucks periods and commas inside the closing quotation mark, whether or not they belong to the quoted words. It is a typesetter's habit from the days of fragile metal type rather than a logical rule, and it is followed almost without exception in the United States. British style puts those same marks outside unless they stood in the original, which is why it is called logical punctuation.

Semicolons and colons behave logically on both sides of the Atlantic, and always go outside the closing quote. Question marks and exclamation points go wherever the question or the shout belongs: inside when the quoted words ask, outside when the surrounding sentence asks. Technical writers often borrow the British habit for commands and code, because a comma swallowed into a quoted command looks like part of what the reader is supposed to type.

Example: 'He muttered fine, then slammed the door.' The comma is the narrator's and not the mutterer's, and American style still puts it inside.
quotation-marks-american-vs-british-punc.title: Quotation Marks: American vs British Punctuation Placement

redundancy-atm-machine-pin-number-advanc.context_blurb:
A phrase is redundant when one word already contains the other's meaning. Acronyms are the usual culprits, because a speaker forgets what the letters stand for and adds the last one again. An ATM machine is an automated teller machine machine. A PIN number is a personal identification number number. Wordplay fans call it RAS syndrome, a joke name whose own expansion ends in syndrome syndrome.

Ordinary phrases do it too. Planning is already about what has not happened yet, so advance planning adds nothing. A gift is already free. History is already past, and a result already comes at the end. Careful planning, by contrast, is not redundant, because careful adds real information. That is the test: cut the suspect word and ask whether the meaning shrank.

Example: 'At seven a.m. in the morning the host gave his own personal opinion.' Morning is already inside a.m., and an opinion you give is already yours, so the sentence can drop four words and lose nothing.
redundancy-atm-machine-pin-number-advanc.title: Redundancy: ATM Machine, PIN Number, Advance Planning

reflexive-pronouns-myself-is-not-a-fancy.context_blurb:
A reflexive pronoun ends in -self or -selves and has exactly two legitimate jobs. First, it points back to the subject of its own clause, when the doer and the receiver are the same person: she cut herself, he talks to himself. Second, it adds emphasis beside a noun, insisting that this person and not a deputy did the thing: the headmaster himself answered the door.

Everything else is politeness gone wrong. People reach for myself because me sounds blunt and I sounds grand, but a reflexive cannot stand in for either. Strip the sentence down to one person and your ear will tell you which you need. 'Send the report to Sarah or myself' becomes 'send the report to myself', which nobody would ever say, so the word wanted is me. 'The manager and myself will attend' becomes 'myself will attend', so the word wanted is I.

Example: 'Between you and me, I fixed the gate myself.' One plain object pronoun, one honest emphatic.
reflexive-pronouns-myself-is-not-a-fancy.title: Reflexive Pronouns: Myself Is Not a Fancy 'Me' or 'I'

register-casual-formal-academic-technica.context_blurb:
Register is the level of formality a piece of writing picks for its audience. Casual register uses contractions, slang and half sentences, and it is right for a group chat or a note on the fridge. Formal register keeps its full forms and its manners, which is what a letter to a stranger who might employ you requires. Academic register states a claim and defines its terms. Technical register names parts and processes exactly, in the vocabulary of people who already know the field. Literary register reaches for image and rhythm, as Carl Sandburg did in 1916 when he wrote that the fog comes on little cat feet.

No register is better than the others, and the mistake is always a mismatch. Slang in an essay and legal stiffness in a text message fail in the same way.

Example: 'This paper examines how sleep affects memory' and 'basically this is gonna be about how sleep matters a bunch' make the same claim, and only one of them belongs in a school essay.
register-casual-formal-academic-technica.title: Register: Casual, Formal, Academic, Technical, Literary

relative-clauses-verb-agrees-with-the-no.context_blurb:
A relative pronoun, who or that, borrows its number from the noun it points back to, and the verb inside the clause then has to match that noun rather than the subject at the front of the sentence. So hunt for the word the pronoun refers to, which is usually the noun standing immediately in front of it.

That is why a phrase shaped one of the X who takes a plural verb: who points at the plural X, not at the word one. Add the word only and the arithmetic changes, because the only one of the X who singles out a lone person, so who now points at one and the verb goes singular. With a phrase such as a list of items or a box of nails, decide by meaning, and ask which noun is really doing what the clause describes.

Example: 'He is one of the farmers who rise before dawn, though he is the only one of the farmers who milks by hand.' Many farmers rise; exactly one milks.
relative-clauses-verb-agrees-with-the-no.title: Relative Clauses: Verb Agrees with the Noun WHO/THAT Refers to

restrictive-vs-non-restrictive-clauses-t.context_blurb:
Two commas around a clause are a promise to a reader: the words between them can be lifted straight out and the sentence will still say who or what is meant. No commas is the opposite promise, that these words are doing the identifying, and that removing them leaves a reader asking which one.

So the marks carry the arithmetic. 'The dog that bit me ran off' implies there were other dogs, and the clause picks one of them out. 'The dog, which bit me, ran off' says there is one dog in the story and the biting is extra news about him. A proper noun almost always takes the commas, since a city or a named brother needs no further identifying.

Example: 'The players who cheated were suspended' suspends only the cheats. 'The players, who cheated, were suspended' confesses that the whole squad cheated and the whole squad is out. Read the sentence with the clause deleted, and whichever meaning survives is the one your commas chose.
restrictive-vs-non-restrictive-clauses-t.title: Restrictive vs Non-Restrictive Clauses (That vs Which)

run-on-sentences-fused-sentences-no-punc.context_blurb:
A fused sentence, usually called a run-on, is two complete sentences crashed together with nothing at all between them. 'The rain fell birds took shelter' is one: both halves have a subject and a verb, both could stand alone, and no mark separates them. Length has nothing to do with it, since a very long sentence can be perfectly punctuated and a six-word one can be fused.

Count the independent clauses first, then pick one of four repairs. Use a full stop. Use a semicolon. Use a comma plus one of the and-but-or family. Or put a leaning word such as because or when in front of one half so it depends on the other. Leaving it alone is not a repair, and a bare comma is not one either, because that produces the near relative of this error, in which one weak mark is asked to do a full stop's work.

Example: 'The power went out we found the candles.' Two clauses and no mark, so insert a semicolon, or write 'so we found the candles'.
run-on-sentences-fused-sentences-no-punc.title: Run-on Sentences (Fused Sentences): No Punctuation at All

second-person-and-imperatives-in-instruc.context_blurb:
The imperative is the command form of a verb, and its subject is an unwritten you. Stir the sauce. Turn left at the lights. Nothing is missing from either sentence: the reader is the subject, and English simply leaves him unsaid.

That is why instructions are written this way. A recipe or a manual that says one should do a thing puts a stranger between the reader and the task, and a passive version hides who is supposed to act at all. The imperative sounds like somebody standing at your elbow, which is exactly the tone a set of steps wants. Second person does the same work when a full sentence is needed: you press the red button twice.

Formal writing softens the command on purpose. Academic and legal prose prefer should plus a verb, because a statute addressed to thousands of readers cannot bark at any one of them.

Example: 'Hold the lid down, then count to ten.' Two commands, no subject printed, and no doubt about who does the holding.
second-person-and-imperatives-in-instruc.title: Second Person and Imperatives in Instructions

semantic-shift-nice-used-to-mean-foolish.context_blurb:
Words drift. You can read a sentence from 1600 and take away the opposite of what the writer meant, because the words have quietly changed jobs since. Nice came through Latin nescius, not knowing, and in Middle English it meant foolish or ignorant. Silly began as the Old English saelig, blessed and happy. Awful once meant full of awe, which is why a writer could pay God that compliment. Girl covered a youngster of either sex, so a boy could be one.

Scholars sort the drift into four patterns. Narrowing shrinks what a word covers, as meat did on its way from any food at all to flesh alone. Widening does the reverse, which is how a holy day became any day off school. Amelioration raises a word's status, as knight did in travelling from servant boy to armoured noble. Pejoration drags a word down.

Example: villain once named a farm worker tied to a country estate. Pejoration carried it the rest of the way.
semantic-shift-nice-used-to-mean-foolish.title: Semantic Shift: Nice Used to Mean Foolish

semicolons-as-super-commas-in-complex-li.context_blurb:
A semicolon can act as a super-comma. When the items in a list already carry commas of their own, ordinary commas between the items stop marking the joins, and a reader can no longer see where one item ends and the next begins. Promote the separators to semicolons and the structure comes back.

The classic case is a list of city-and-country pairs, where comma-only punctuation makes it impossible to tell whether each country belongs to the city in front of it or stands as an item of its own. The same thing happens with a list of full dates, or a list of people followed by their job titles. The rule is mechanical: if any item contains a comma, every separator in that list becomes a semicolon, including the one before the final and.

Example: 'The judges were Marcus Hale, a baker from Leeds; Anna Petrov, a chemist; and Sam Oduya, who had never judged anything before.' Three judges, three semicolons, and nothing left to guess at.
semicolons-as-super-commas-in-complex-li.title: Semicolons As Super-Commas in Complex Lists

semicolons-before-conjunctive-adverbs-ho.context_blurb:
However, therefore, moreover, nevertheless and consequently are conjunctive adverbs. They feel like joining words, but grammatically they are adverbs, and an adverb cannot hold two sentences together. Put a plain comma in front of one and you have joined two sentences with a mark far too weak for the job.

So the pattern has three cases. Joining two independent clauses, the adverb wants a semicolon in front of it and a comma behind it. Opening a fresh sentence after a full stop, it wants only the comma behind it. Sitting inside a single clause as an aside, it takes a comma on each side, because there is no join to make. Real coordinating conjunctions, the and-but-or family, behave differently and take an ordinary comma in front.

Example: 'The bridge was closed; therefore, we drove around the lake. We were, however, two hours late.' The first mark holds two sentences together, and the pair in the second sentence merely sets off an interruption.
semicolons-before-conjunctive-adverbs-ho.title: Semicolons Before Conjunctive Adverbs (However, Therefore)

semicolons-joining-independent-clauses.context_blurb:
A semicolon is a soft full stop. It links two complete sentences whose ideas belong together and says: these could stand apart, but read them as one thought. Both halves must be able to stand alone, and that is the whole test.

Three mistakes follow from ignoring it. A leaning half, one opening with because, although or when, cannot sit after a semicolon, because it is not a sentence. A conjunction cannot follow one either: if you have already written and, then a comma was all you needed. And a semicolon is not a heavy comma, so it never separates a subject from its verb or an adjective from its noun. The only other job it holds is separating the items of a list when those items already contain commas.

Example: 'The gate was locked; we climbed the wall.' Cover either half with your hand and what remains is still a sentence, which is the only licence a semicolon ever requires.
semicolons-joining-independent-clauses.title: Semicolons: Joining Independent Clauses

sentence-fragments-missing-the-subject.context_blurb:
Every English sentence needs somebody or something doing the verb. Drop that noun and what is left still looks like a sentence, with a capital letter at the front and a full stop at the back, but a reader finishes it asking who. 'Ran quickly down the street' names the running and never names the runner.

This fragment is common because the subject feels obvious. A writer has just named his cousin, so the next three sentences carry on about what she did and each one quietly loses her. Diary entries and scribbled notes lean on the same habit. The cure is two words long: ask who or what did the verb, and if the answer appears nowhere in the sentence, put it in. Commands are the one real exception, since an order already carries an unwritten you.

Example: 'Woke up late. Missed the bus. Walked to school.' Three verbs and not one subject, so hand each sentence back its he or she.
sentence-fragments-missing-the-subject.title: Sentence Fragments: Missing the Subject

sentence-fragments-missing-the-verb.context_blurb:
A string of words can be long, vivid and still not a sentence, because length is not the test. A verb is. A noun with every adjective you own hung on it remains a noun, which is why 'The huge orange cat on the windowsill' hands you a picture and never tells you what the animal does.

Two shapes cause most of the trouble. The first is a swollen noun phrase, which fools the eye because it fills a whole line. The second is a chain of prepositional phrases, all scenery and no action, like a camera panning across a garage and never finding anybody in it. The repair is to add the missing verb rather than more detail. Watch an -ing word standing on its own as well, since a participle is not a working verb until a helper such as is or was arrives to prop it up.

Example: 'A loud crash in the kitchen at two in the morning.' Nothing happens yet. Add woke me and the words finally do something.
sentence-fragments-missing-the-verb.title: Sentence Fragments: Missing the Verb

sentence-fragments-subordinate-clause-st.context_blurb:
A subordinate clause has a subject and a verb and still cannot stand alone, because the word at its front makes it lean on a sentence that has not arrived yet. 'Because it was late' passes every other test and leaves a reader waiting for the rest of the news.

Learn the leaning words and you will spot the fragment from across the room: because, when, if, although, until, while, unless, since, after and before. Two repairs work. Attach a main clause, which is what the stranded clause was asking for all along, or delete the leaning word so that what remains is a sentence in its own right. A reduced version, with the subject and the helper verb left out, dangles in the same way and takes the same treatment.

Example: 'While walking to the shop.' Who was walking, and what happened? Finish it as 'While walking to the shop, I found a five-pound note', and the opening now leans on something solid.
sentence-fragments-subordinate-clause-st.title: Sentence Fragments: Subordinate Clause Stranded

sentence-types-simple-compound-complex-c.context_blurb:
There are four sentence types, and all you need is a head count of clauses. An independent clause can stand alone. A leaning clause cannot, because it opens with a word such as because or when, or begins with who or which and describes a noun.

So count. One independent clause by itself is a simple sentence, however many adjectives it drags along. Two or more independent clauses, joined by a comma plus a conjunction or by a semicolon, make a compound sentence. One independent clause plus at least one leaning clause makes it complex, and a who or which clause tucked into the middle counts as the leaning one. Two independent clauses plus a leaning clause make a sentence that is compound and complex at once.

Example: 'Although the tide was out, we launched the boat, and the dog swam beside us.' One clause that cannot stand alone, two that can, so the sentence belongs to the longest category. Mark the clauses first, then name the type.
sentence-types-simple-compound-complex-c.title: Sentence Types: Simple, Compound, Complex, Compound-Complex

sentence-variety-and-rhythm.context_blurb:
Sentences of one length, lined up in a row, put a reader to sleep whatever they happen to say. Rhythm comes from contrast. Short sentences hit, medium ones carry the load, and a long one can unfold a whole scene so long as four more of its kind do not follow it.

Openings matter as much as lengths. If every sentence begins with the same word or the same shape, a paragraph flattens even when the lengths differ, which is why Strunk warned writers in 1918 against stringing loose clauses together one after another. Gary Provost made the point unforgettably in 1985 by writing a passage of identical short sentences, so that a reader feels the monotony before being told about it. Variety is not the same virtue as concision, either. Cutting dead words is a separate job, and a paragraph can be tight and dull at the same time.

Example: 'We walked for an hour past the quarry, past the shuttered petrol station, past the field where the horses stood with their backs to the wind. Then it rained.' Twenty-eight words, then three.
sentence-variety-and-rhythm.title: Sentence Variety and Rhythm

shall-vs-will-the-nearly-extinct-distinc.context_blurb:
The old British rule had a neat shape. For a plain statement about the future, shall went with I and we, while will went with you, he, she and it. To add force the pair swapped over: will with I or we became a declaration of intent, and shall with you or he became a promise or a command handed down from above. That is why a fairy godmother tells Cinderella she shall go to the ball. The word carries authority, not a forecast.

American English dropped the distinction long ago and uses will for almost every future. Shall survives in a few fixed phrases, in polite offers, and above all in legal drafting, where it is not about the future at all: in a contract or a statute it imposes a duty on whoever is named.

Example: 'We will finish by Friday' is a resolution. 'You shall finish by Friday' is an order, which is why the second one sounds so strange coming from a friend.
shall-vs-will-the-nearly-extinct-distinc.title: Shall vs Will: The Nearly-Extinct Distinction

should-of-could-of-would-of-the-impossib.context_blurb:
There is no verb of. Of is a preposition, and a preposition cannot follow a modal, so should of, could of, would of, might of and must of are all impossible on paper. The word wanted is have, every single time.

The error is an honest one, because the contractions sound exactly like the mistake. Say the shortened form of should have out loud at ordinary speed and your ear hears the preposition; spelling it that way just writes the mispronunciation down. The written test is quick. Expand the contraction, and whatever follows a modal has to be a verb, which of can never be. Novelists do spell it the wrong way inside dialogue on purpose, because it tells a reader how a character talks, and that is a deliberate choice rather than a licence.

Example: 'I would of called, but I must of lost your number.' Two slips in one breath, and both of them want the one little verb that is allowed to follow a modal.
should-of-could-of-would-of-the-impossib.title: Should of / Could of / Would of — The Impossible Verb

single-vs-double-quotation-marks-and-nes.context_blurb:
American practice opens a quotation with double marks and switches to single marks for a quotation inside it. Traditional British practice does the reverse, starting with single marks and switching to double within, although many modern British publishers have gone over to the American arrangement. Either system works, provided you alternate: outer, then inner, then back to the outer kind if a third quotation turns up inside the second.

Single marks have two other uses worth knowing. A writer who wants to hold a word at arm's length puts scare quotes around it, signalling that the label is somebody else's and that he does not accept it. And two specialist fields reserve the single mark on purpose: linguists use it when they give the meaning of a word, and gardeners use it around the name of a cultivated plant variety.

Example: "She said, 'he told me to walk it off,' and shrugged." The outer pair belongs to the narrator and the inner pair to the man she quotes.
single-vs-double-quotation-marks-and-nes.title: Single vs Double Quotation Marks and Nested Quotes

slashes-and-or-dates-and-line-breaks-in-.context_blurb:
A slash means alternatives. The phrase and/or is the one common case where it means alternatives plus the option of both, which is why lawyers like it and editors do not. Pass/fail, on/off and he/she all work the same way: two choices, one mark, no spaces around it.

The slash also separates the parts of a numeric date, and there it turns dangerous. American order runs month first, so 7/4/1776 is the fourth of July. British order runs day first, so the same three numbers mean the seventh of April. The international standard sidesteps the quarrel by going from the largest unit down, year then month then day, joined with hyphens instead of slashes, which has the happy effect of sorting correctly on a computer.

One more job: when poetry is quoted inside a paragraph, a slash with a space on each side marks where a line ended in the original.

Example: 'Two roads diverged in a yellow wood, / And sorry I could not travel both.' The mark stands where the poet's line broke.
slashes-and-or-dates-and-line-breaks-in-.title: Slashes: And/or, Dates, and Line Breaks in Poetry

spoonerism-the-reverend-who-swapped-his-.context_blurb:
A spoonerism swaps the opening sounds of two nearby words. Reverend William Archibald Spooner taught at New College, Oxford, around the turn of the twentieth century, and the slip carries his name: the tongue reaches the second word's consonant first, and the phrase comes out inside out. Tell a friend he has suffered a blushing crow when you meant a crushing blow and you have made one.

Two warnings. Most of the lines credited to Spooner were invented by delighted students, so the honest wording is that they are attributed to him rather than recorded from him. And a spoonerism is not a malapropism. The swap moves sounds between two real words, while a malapropism replaces a word altogether with a different one that sounds similar, which is how a character ends up praising somebody as the pineapple of politeness.

Example: a guest meant to raise his glass to the dear old queen and toasted the queer old dean instead. Same sounds, same words, wrong order.
spoonerism-the-reverend-who-swapped-his-.title: Spoonerism: The Reverend Who Swapped His Sounds

squinting-modifiers-the-adverb-that-face.context_blurb:
A squinting modifier sits between two verbs and looks at both of them, so a reader cannot tell which one it belongs to. 'Students who study rarely fail' is the classic shape: the adverb may describe how often they study or how often they fail, and the two readings say opposite things about the value of homework.

Three modifier faults are worth keeping apart. A squinting modifier has two possible owners in the sentence and no way to choose between them. A misplaced modifier has landed clearly beside the wrong word, which is how a telescope ends up in the wrong hands. A dangling modifier has no owner at all, because the noun it describes never appears.

The repair for the squinting kind is position, not punctuation. Shift the word or phrase until it touches only the verb you meant, or rebuild the sentence so the ambiguity has nowhere left to hide.

Example: 'He promised on Tuesday to call her.' Did the promising happen on Tuesday, or the call? Move the phrase to the front or to the very end and the question disappears.
squinting-modifiers-the-adverb-that-face.title: Squinting Modifiers: The Adverb That Faces Both Ways

stationary-vs-stationery-standing-still-.context_blurb:
Two spellings, one pronunciation, and only the vowel in the last syllable to tell them apart. The -ary word means standing still: a parked car, an exercise bike that goes nowhere, a clock that does not budge. The -ery word means writing materials: paper, envelopes, cards.

Hang it on a letter. Envelope begins with E, and envelopes are the things in the drawer, so the E spelling is the paper one. The other spelling carries an A, as in stay where you are. Both words descend from station, a standing place, and the split happened in the Middle Ages, when a stationer was a bookseller licensed to trade from a fixed stall instead of wandering about with a pack. The goods on his stall took his name.

Example: 'She sat on the stationary bike and wrote her thank-you notes on her best stationery.' The bike goes nowhere, and the paper gets a stamp.
stationary-vs-stationery-standing-still-.title: Stationary vs Stationery — Standing Still vs Writing Paper

subject-verb-agreement-basics-singular-v.context_blurb:
A verb agrees with its subject and with nothing else. One dog barks, two dogs bark. The whole difficulty lies in finding the subject, because English likes to park other nouns between it and the verb.

Cross out every prepositional phrase with your finger. In a phrase such as a list of items, a bouquet of flowers or a box of nails, the subject is the list, the bouquet and the box, so the verb stays singular however many items, flowers or nails get mentioned. Three other shapes catch people out. In a sentence beginning with there, the subject comes after the verb, so look to the right of it. A sum of money, a span of time or a distance counts as one quantity and takes a singular verb. And a piece of arithmetic is a single statement, which is why two and two makes four.

Example: 'The crate of oranges was heavy.' One crate, one verb, and the oranges are only passing through.
subject-verb-agreement-basics-singular-v.title: Subject-Verb Agreement Basics (Singular vs Plural)

subjunctive-mood-if-i-were-you-vs-if-i-w.context_blurb:
Mood is the attitude a verb takes. The indicative states what is, the imperative orders, and the subjunctive deals with what is not, or not yet. English has worn its subjunctive down to a few places, and were is the survivor everybody notices.

Two patterns are worth learning. In a hypothetical that is contrary to fact, the verb takes were for every subject, which is why the polite formula begins if I were. A wish behaves the same way, since wishing is contrary to fact by definition. The second pattern is the demanding one: after insist, demand, require, suggest or ask that, the verb drops to its bare form with no ending at all, so a teacher insists that a pupil be on time rather than is on time. That form is fading from casual speech, where should has taken over the job.

Example: 'The coach demanded that every substitute be ready, and said he wished the pitch were dry.' One bare verb for the demand, one were for the impossibility.
subjunctive-mood-if-i-were-you-vs-if-i-w.title: Subjunctive Mood: 'If I WERE You' vs 'If I WAS You'

tense-sequence-reported-speech-shifts-ba.context_blurb:
When you report what somebody said instead of quoting him, the tense inside steps back one notch, because the saying itself is already in the past. A present verb goes to the past. A past verb goes to the form with had. Will becomes would, can becomes could, may becomes might, and must usually becomes had to.

Pronouns and time words shift along with the tenses. I becomes he or she, here becomes there, tomorrow becomes the next day, and this becomes that. The step back is not always required. If the thing said is still true, a writer may leave the present alone, which is why a report of a science lesson can say the teacher explained that water boils at a hundred degrees. And if the reporting verb is itself in the present, nothing moves at all.

Example: he said, 'I am leaving tomorrow and I will write.' Reported afterwards, that becomes: he said he was leaving the next day and would write.
tense-sequence-reported-speech-shifts-ba.title: Tense Sequence: Reported Speech Shifts Backward

text-speak-vs-formal-register-lol-imo-ii.context_blurb:
Text-speak is the shorthand that grew up around phone keyboards: initials standing in for whole clauses, dropped vowels, and spellings that exist only to save thumb work. A reader who knows the code decodes it instantly. A reader who does not simply stops, and that is the whole argument about where the shorthand belongs.

Match it to the audience rather than to your own comfort. A group chat, a reply to a friend and a casual post can carry as much of it as both sides enjoy. An essay, a job application, a report, or a letter to anybody who can say no cannot, because the shorthand tells that reader you did not think him worth a whole word. Emojis sit on the same line. The test is never whether a form is lazy; it is whether your reader shares it.

Example: 'idk, the temp was prob too low' carries the same information as 'the temperature was probably too low', and only one of the two belongs in a laboratory report.
text-speak-vs-formal-register-lol-imo-ii.title: Text-Speak vs Formal Register: LOL, IMO, IIRC

that-vs-which-restrictive-vs-non-restric.context_blurb:
American editors pair the pronoun with the punctuation. A clause that identifies which one gets that and no commas. A clause that merely adds news gets which, with a comma at each end. The two halves of the convention travel together, so a comma in front of that is nearly always a mistake, and a which with no commas round it usually wants to be that.

British practice is looser. British writers use which for both kinds of clause and let the commas do the work on their own, which is why an English newspaper sentence can look wrong to an American eye and be perfectly correct at home. People take who in either country, and the comma rule does not change for them.

Example: 'My brother who lives in Paris sent a postcard' quietly tells a reader that other brothers exist and that the Paris one is being singled out. Add two commas and the family shrinks to one brother who happens to live abroad.
that-vs-which-restrictive-vs-non-restric.title: That vs Which — Restrictive vs Non-Restrictive

the-comma-splice-two-sentences-glued-wit.context_blurb:
Here is the detector. Cover the comma with your thumb and read each side as its own sentence. If both sides stand up on their own, a comma is too weak to hold them and you have a splice. 'She loved coffee, he preferred tea' fails the test twice over.

Which repair you choose changes the meaning, so choose on purpose. A full stop separates the two ideas. A semicolon keeps them touching, which suits a pair of events that land on top of each other. Adding a conjunction names the relationship, since and adds, but contrasts and so explains. Making one side lean on the other with because or when ranks one idea under its neighbour. One exception is genuine: three or four very short, tightly parallel clauses may take commas as a deliberate rhythm, which is how the famous translation of Caesar's boast, I came, I saw, I conquered, is punctuated.

Example: 'The lights went out, nobody moved.' Thumb over the comma, hear two sentences, and reach for a semicolon.
the-comma-splice-two-sentences-glued-wit.title: The Comma Splice: Two Sentences Glued with Just a Comma

the-grandma-comma-and-other-missing-comm.context_blurb:
A comma of direct address, called a vocative comma, separates the person you are speaking to from whatever you are saying about him. Leave it out and that person becomes an ingredient. 'Let's eat, Grandma!' calls her to the table; 'Let's eat Grandma!' puts her on it, and one small mark is the whole difference between an invitation and a recipe.

The same gap swallows items out of a list. A magazine cover once announced that a celebrity cook found inspiration in cooking her family and her dog, when a pair of commas would have turned one horror into three separate joys. An introductory phrase needs its comma too, or the sentence runs straight on into the next noun and devours it.

Example: 'While eating, the cat watched television.' Drop that comma and the opening phrase grabs the cat as its object, so somebody unnamed is now eating the animal. Read your sentence aloud and listen for who is being addressed and who is being served.
the-grandma-comma-and-other-missing-comm.title: The Grandma Comma and Other Missing-Comma Horrors

the-oxford-comma-strippers-jfk-and-stali.context_blurb:
The Oxford comma, also called the serial comma, is the one that sits in front of the final and in a list. Writers argue about it because it is genuinely optional: Chicago and most book publishers use it every time, while the Associated Press and most newspapers leave it out unless the sentence would collapse without it.

The collapse is the entertaining part. Take the mark out of a guest list running the strippers, JFK and Stalin, and the last two names stop being guests and start describing the dancers. A dedication to my parents, Ayn Rand and God, does the same thing to a writer's family tree. It can also bite the other way, since a comma in front of a name can turn that name into an appositive and quietly make the mother and the famous novelist one person. In 2018 a Maine dairy paid about five million in back overtime because a state law listed exempt jobs without the mark.

Example: 'We invited the clowns, my aunt and the mayor.' Add the comma and three guests arrive; leave it out and your aunt has a red nose.
the-oxford-comma-strippers-jfk-and-stali.title: The Oxford Comma: Strippers, JFK, and Stalin

the-rare-punctuation-marks-interrobang-p.context_blurb:
English has a handful of marks that almost nobody uses and everybody has seen. The interrobang is a question mark and an exclamation point printed on top of each other, for a sentence that asks and gasps at once; an advertising man named Martin Speckter proposed it in 1962 and it never quite caught on. The pilcrow is the backwards P that marks where a paragraph begins, still working away in legal and liturgical texts and visible in a word processor when you switch on the hidden characters. The section sign, two interlocking S shapes, points at a numbered section of a statute, and doubling it means several sections at once.

Guillemets are the little arrowheads that serve as quotation marks in French, Russian and a number of other European languages. And where footnotes are marked with symbols instead of numbers, the traditional order runs asterisk, dagger, double dagger, section mark, parallels, number sign.

Example: a citation pointing at two sections of a law prints the section sign twice before the numbers, and a reader who knows the mark reads it as a plural.
the-rare-punctuation-marks-interrobang-p.title: The Rare Punctuation Marks: Interrobang, Pilcrow, Guillemets

the-vocative-comma-lets-eat-grandma.context_blurb:
When you speak to a person by name, that name is fenced off from the sentence around it, and the number of commas depends on where the name sits. At the end of a sentence it takes one in front of it. At the start it takes one behind it. In the middle it takes one on each side, and forgetting the second one is the commonest half-finished version of the rule.

Two neighbours look similar and are doing other work. An interjection such as well, oh or look also takes a comma, but it is not addressing anybody. An appositive renames a noun instead of calling out to it, which is why my brother Mark and my brother, Mark, differ in how many brothers exist, a separate question from whether you are talking to him.

Example: 'Thanks, Dad.' 'Dad, thanks.' 'I did say, Dad, thanks.' One comma, then one comma, then two, and in all three the word Dad is being spoken to rather than spoken about.
the-vocative-comma-lets-eat-grandma.title: The Vocative Comma: 'Let's Eat, Grandma!'

then-vs-than-time-vs-comparison.context_blurb:
Then is about time or sequence. Than is about comparison. Nothing else is at stake, and neither spelling is British or American.

Hang it on the vowel. The E in then matches the E in time and in sequence: first this, then that, back then, if-then. The A in than matches the A in compare: bigger than, rather than, no sooner than. If the sentence sets two things side by side and measures them, you want the comparison word; if it is moving along a clock, you want the other one.

One related argument is worth knowing. Different from is safe everywhere. Different than is standard American English in front of a whole clause, as in different than I expected, while British writers prefer from throughout and often say different to in speech.

Example: 'She is taller then her brother' accidentally claims that she grew after he did, which is a story rather than a measurement. Change the one letter and she is simply the taller of the two.
then-vs-than-time-vs-comparison.title: Then vs Than — Time vs Comparison

there-is-there-are-agreement-with-the-no.context_blurb:
A sentence that opens with there has no subject at the front. The word is only a placeholder, which grammarians call an expletive or a dummy subject, and the real subject arrives after the verb. So look to the right of the verb to pick its form: the noun that follows is the one the verb has to match, singular for singular and plural for plural.

That is why careful writing uses the plural verb in front of a plural noun, however natural the contraction sounds out loud. Everybody says there's two reasons, because the contraction slips out before the speaker knows how many reasons are coming, and nobody writes it that way on purpose. A compound subject after there is the one messy case, and the clean escape is to put the subject first and drop the placeholder altogether.

Example: 'There is a bicycle in the hall, and there are three more in the shed.' Each verb takes its cue from the noun after it rather than from the word in front.
there-is-there-are-agreement-with-the-no.title: There Is / There Are: Agreement with the Noun After

there-their-theyre-the-three-way-apostro.context_blurb:
Three spellings, one sound, three jobs, and each has a hidden word inside it to give the game away. There contains here, and both are about place. Their contains heir, and an heir is somebody who inherits, so that spelling is about owning. The third has an apostrophe, and an apostrophe always marks a missing letter, which here is the A of are.

So the test is substitution. Read you are, or rather they are, into the slot: if the sentence survives, the apostrophe form is right. If the sentence is pointing at a place, use the one hiding here. If something belongs to more than one person, use the one hiding heir. All three can turn up in a single breath, and getting two right and one wrong is the usual result.

Example: 'Their coats are over there because they're staying the night.' Owning, then placing, then shortening, and each of the three words is doing a job the other two cannot.
there-their-theyre-the-three-way-apostro.title: There, Their, They're — The Three-Way Apostrophe Trap

time-flies-like-an-arrow-parsing-ambigui.context_blurb:
A parsing ambiguity happens when one string of words can be carved up in two ways and both are perfectly grammatical. English leans hard on word order and barely inflects its words, so a noun can look exactly like a verb, and a reader has to guess which job each word is doing.

The famous pair proves it. In the line about time and an arrow, flies is the verb and like makes a comparison. In the line about the banana, the same two words have swapped jobs: flies joins with fruit to name a small insect, and like becomes the verb that says what the insects enjoy. Nothing is misspelled and nothing is out of place; only the parse has moved. 'They are cooking apples' pulls the same trick, since cooking can be what somebody is doing or what sort of apple is meant, and no punctuation will settle it. Context does.

Example: 'The chicken is ready to eat.' Is dinner served, or is the bird hungry? Both parses are legal, and that is the whole joke.
time-flies-like-an-arrow-parsing-ambigui.title: Time Flies Like an Arrow: Parsing Ambiguity

time-flies-like-an-arrow-the-parsing-amb.context_blurb:
Wordplay comes in families, and four of them get mixed up. A parsing pun sets two clauses side by side in the same shape and then re-cuts the second one, so every word keeps its spelling and changes its job. A garden-path sentence does something else: it leads you into one reading and then forces you to back up and rebuild, which is what happens in the sentence about the horse raced past the barn fell. A spoonerism swaps the opening sounds of two words. A malapropism swaps in a whole wrong word that happens to sound similar.

The insect half of the famous arrow joke works on a noun-noun compound, where two nouns lock together and behave as a single noun. English is full of them: ice cream, computer chip, paper clip. Hearing the first noun as a modifier instead of a subject is what flips the sentence over. The gag is usually credited to Groucho Marx, which is almost certainly wrong; it surfaces in print in the 1960s in writing about machine translation.

Example: hearing fruit flies as one small creature rather than as fruit in flight is the entire pivot.
time-flies-like-an-arrow-the-parsing-amb.title: Time Flies Like an Arrow: The Parsing-Ambiguity Pun

titles-of-works-the-new-york-times-is-a-.context_blurb:
A title names one thing, so it takes a singular verb however plural it looks. Great Expectations is a novel. Little Women appeared in 1868. The New York Times reports a story, because a newspaper is one publication even though its name ends in an s. A film, an album, a play and a single episode all behave the same way.

Two neighbours work differently. A plural proper name that is not the title of a work keeps its plural verb, which is why the Beatles were four men from Liverpool while Coldplay is one band with a singular-looking name. And a word ending in -ics is usually singular when it names a field of study, so mathematics takes a singular verb and so does physics, although some of those words go plural when they mean somebody's opinions or conduct rather than the subject itself.

Example: 'Star Wars is a franchise, and the prequels are still argued about.' The title is one work; the films inside it are many, and the verbs follow.
titles-of-works-the-new-york-times-is-a-.title: Titles of Works: 'The New York Times IS a Newspaper'

to-too-two-three-tiny-words-three-jobs.context_blurb:
Three words, one sound, three jobs. Two is the number, and it keeps the W that runs through twin, twice and twelve. To is the little word in front of a place or a verb: to the shop, to run. The third one means also, or else it means more of something than you want.

The extra O is the hook worth keeping. That spelling carries one more O than it needs, and the spare letter is the excess the word describes, which covers the sense of in addition as well. The number is the spelling nobody misuses; the trouble is always between the other two, so read also or excessively into the slot and see whether the sentence still stands.

A small point of style: the comma in front of that word at the end of a sentence is optional. Both versions are correct, and the comma buys a tiny pause rather than obeying a rule.

Example: 'He walked to the shop to buy two lemons, and came home with a melon too.' Direction, purpose, number and addition, in that order.
to-too-two-three-tiny-words-three-jobs.title: To, Too, Two — Three Tiny Words, Three Jobs

two-spaces-after-a-period-the-zombie-typ.context_blurb:
One space after a full stop. Chicago and every other modern style guide say so, and the proportional type in a word processor already builds the right amount of air into the period itself.

The two-space habit came from the typewriter. Typewriter letters were monospaced, so a thin i took up the same slot as a fat m, and a single space after a sentence looked cramped. Typists were trained from the 1890s onward to hit the bar twice, and the training outlived the machines. That is what a zombie rule is: a rule still obeyed after the reason for it has died. Never splitting an infinitive is another. A 2018 reading experiment at Skidmore College found a small benefit for the double space, but it tested only a monospaced font, so it never answered the question for the type everybody actually reads.

Example: type three spaces in a row into a web page and the browser prints one, because the layout rules collapse any run of whitespace. Even the machine votes for a single space.
two-spaces-after-a-period-the-zombie-typ.title: Two Spaces After a Period? The Zombie Typewriter Rule

verb-mood-indicative-imperative-subjunct.context_blurb:
Mood is not tone. It is the shape a verb takes to show what kind of statement is being made, and English uses four of them.

The indicative is the workhorse: it states that something is the case, and asks whether something is the case. The imperative gives an order, with the subject you left unwritten. The subjunctive handles what is not the case, which is why it turns up in wishes, in hypotheticals and after verbs of demanding. The conditional pairs an if-clause with a would-clause and lays out a consequence that hangs on something unreal. Only two of the four still have special forms, since the imperative drops its subject and the subjunctive uses were or a bare verb; the others are built from ordinary tenses and helpers.

Example: 'The kettle is boiling' states. 'Boil the kettle' orders. 'I wish the kettle were quicker' wishes. 'If the kettle boiled faster, we would catch the train' supposes. Four moods, one kettle, and the verb form tells a reader which is which.
verb-mood-indicative-imperative-subjunct.title: Verb Mood: Indicative, Imperative, Subjunctive, Conditional

verb-tense-consistency-do-not-jump-tense.context_blurb:
Pick a tense for a passage and hold it. A reader builds a timeline out of your verbs, so a sentence that starts in the past and finishes in the present throws him off the track: the walking has finished and the buying is apparently still going on.

Two shifts are legitimate. A general truth that is still true may stay in the present inside a past-tense passage, which is why you can write that you visited a museum and that it is the largest in the city. And a writer may tell a past story in the present on purpose, a device called the historical present, so that an emperor marches on Moscow in front of the reader rather than behind him. What the device does not allow is drifting: once the march is in the present, the suffering that follows cannot slip back into the past.

Example: 'She walks to the window, opened it, and listens.' Three verbs, two tenses, one seasick reader. Choose either tense and make all three obey it.
verb-tense-consistency-do-not-jump-tense.title: Verb Tense Consistency: Do Not Jump Tenses Mid-Paragraph

who-vs-whom-the-he-him-substitution-tric.context_blurb:
The test is mechanical. Rebuild the clause as a plain statement with he or him in the gap, and whichever pronoun fits gives you the answer: he goes with who, and him goes with the form that carries the same M.

Two traps catch people who already know the trick. First, a preposition always takes the object form, so a letter is addressed to the M word no matter how the rest of the sentence runs. Second, a small inserted clause such as she thought or we hoped changes nothing: lift it out, and if what is left needs a subject for the verb that follows, the subject form stands. That is why a candidate we hoped would win takes the subject form even with those extra words in the way.

Example: 'The tourists ___ she met at the hotel never came back.' Rebuild it as she met them, hear that him fits the slot, and write the form with the M in it.
who-vs-whom-the-he-him-substitution-tric.title: Who vs Whom: The He/him Substitution Trick

who-vs-whom-the-m-means-object.context_blurb:
Who does the acting; whom gets acted upon. The letter M is the whole mnemonic, because the object pronouns him, them and whom all end in it, while the subject pronouns he, they and who do not.

Find the verb inside the clause and ask whether the word is doing that verb or receiving it. Doing means the subject form. Receiving, or sitting after a preposition, means the M form, which is why the standard opening of a letter to a stranger takes it, and why the title Hemingway borrowed from a John Donne meditation takes it too. The famous telephone question runs the other way, since whoever is calling is doing the calling, so the subject form is right however formal the sentence sounds.

Formality matters as well. In speech the M form is fading, and insisting on it can sound starchy; in formal writing it is still expected.

Example: 'She is the friend ___ remembers my birthday.' The gap does the remembering, so it takes the subject form.
who-vs-whom-the-m-means-object.title: Who vs Whom — The M Means Object

whose-vs-whos-the-possessive-pronoun-exc.context_blurb:
The apostrophe in English does two unrelated jobs, and that is the whole source of the confusion. On a noun it shows ownership. On a pronoun it never does. Possessive pronouns refuse the mark altogether: his, hers, ours, yours, theirs, its and whose. So the spelling with the apostrophe cannot be the owning one, because that mark is standing in for a missing letter instead.

Say the long version in your head. The contraction expands to who is or who has, and if the expansion fits, the apostrophe belongs there. If the sentence is asking which person something belongs to, the apostrophe has no business in it at all.

Example: a sign reading 'Who's coat is this?' expands to 'Who is coat is this', which falls over immediately, so the sign wanted the other spelling. 'Who's taken my coat?' expands to 'who has taken my coat' and stands up perfectly. One test, two words, no guessing.
whose-vs-whos-the-possessive-pronoun-exc.title: Whose vs Who's — The Possessive Pronoun Exception, Again

wordy-vs-concise-cut-the-deadweight.context_blurb:
Concise does not mean short. It means that no word is being paid for work it is not doing. A long sentence can be lean, and a six-word one can be padded.

Four kinds of padding account for most of the damage.
