Prepositional stacks swell one word into four, so a phrase built around the fact that is almost always just because, and a phrase built around the event that is just if. Buried verbs hide the action inside an abstract noun, so somebody makes a decision instead of deciding. Hedging openers announce that a point is about to be made and then make it, which means the opener can go entirely. And empty intensifiers pile a word on top of another that already contains it, which is why nothing can be more essential than something else.

Example: 'At this point in time it is important to note that an evaluation of the proposal will be undertaken by the committee.' Strip out all four kinds and the sentence says that the committee is now reviewing the proposal.
wordy-vs-concise-cut-the-deadweight.title: Wordy vs Concise: Cut the Deadweight

your-vs-youre-the-possessive-apostrophe-.context_blurb:
One of these words owns something and the other is two words in a coat. Your is the possessive: your bike, your turn, your fault. The other is a squashed version of you are, and the apostrophe stands exactly where the A used to be.

The swap test settles every case in a second. Read you are into the slot. If the sentence still works, the apostrophe form is right; if it buckles, the possessive is. A birthday card reading YOUR the best expands to your the best, which never finishes its own thought, while a fridge note reading YOU'RE dog is chasing the mailman expands to you are dog, which is worse. The texting spelling ur stands in for both words at once, which is handy on a phone and useless in an essay, where a reader expects the whole word.

Example: 'Your bike is where you're standing.' One possession, one contraction, and a mark sitting in the gap left by a missing letter.
your-vs-youre-the-possessive-apostrophe-.title: Your vs You're — The Possessive-Apostrophe Punchline

zeugma-and-syllepsis-one-verb-incompatib.context_blurb:
Zeugma is one verb doing duty for several objects, and it lands when the objects do not belong together. Alexander Pope used it on a lady who risks a stain on her honour or on her new brocade, which files a moral disaster and a laundry problem under the same accident. Flanders and Swann built a whole line out of a woman who lowered her standards by raising her glass, her courage, her eyes and a young man's hopes: one verb, four objects, and a different sense of raising in every one.

Two names cover this ground and the border between them is argued over. Zeugma is the broad term for the shared-verb trick. Syllepsis is the strict case, where the verb fits each object grammatically while quietly changing its meaning as it travels, and that shift is where the punchline sits.

Example: 'He lost his keys, his temper and his girlfriend in a single afternoon.' Lost does three different jobs, and the third one is the job that stings.
zeugma-and-syllepsis-one-verb-incompatib.title: Zeugma and Syllepsis: One Verb, Incompatible Objects

zombie-rule-never-begin-a-sentence-with-.context_blurb:
Beginning a sentence with and or but breaks no rule of English, and it never did. The prohibition was a classroom convenience invented in the nineteenth century, because children string clauses together with and for pages at a stretch and a teacher wanted a quick way to stop it. The cure got written down as a law, and the law outlived the problem.

The evidence sits on the shelf. Shakespeare does it, the King James translators do it, Austen and Dickens do it, and Chicago notes that as much as a tenth of the sentences in first-rate writing open with a conjunction. Used on purpose, the opener slows a reader down and lands the second thought harder than a comma would.

One nearby mistake is real and worth keeping straight. A sentence that opens with a leaning word such as because or although and never arrives at a main clause is a fragment. The coordinating words carry no such risk.

Example: 'She trained for two years. And she lost in the first round.' Two sentences, one deliberate conjunction, and the blow arrives on time.
zombie-rule-never-begin-a-sentence-with-.title: Zombie Rule: Never Begin a Sentence with And or But

zombie-rule-never-end-a-sentence-with-a-.context_blurb:
Ending a sentence with a preposition is ordinary English and always has been. The superstition began with seventeenth-century writers who admired Latin, where a preposition genuinely cannot be left stranded, and who decided English ought to behave the same way; John Dryden usually gets the blame. English is not Latin, and the rule has no basis in how the language works.

The standard mockery of it is a sentence nobody can read aloud: this is the sort of English up with which I will not put. The line is usually credited to Churchill and almost certainly was not his, but it makes the point, because hauling the preposition forward can wreck a perfectly good sentence.

So the choice is register, not grammar. Formal prose sometimes reads better with the preposition moved, and only when the result sounds unforced. Casual writing should leave the word where the voice put it.

Example: 'Who did you speak to?' and 'To whom did you speak?' are both correct. The first sounds like a person talking; the second sounds like a form to fill in.
zombie-rule-never-end-a-sentence-with-a-.title: Zombie Rule: Never End a Sentence with a Preposition

zombie-rule-never-split-an-infinitive.context_blurb:
An infinitive in English is two words, to plus a verb, and nothing stops an adverb from sitting between them. The ban came from nineteenth-century writers who wanted English to copy Latin, where the infinitive is a single word and so cannot be split at all. Chicago says plainly that the adverb often belongs inside the pair, and that a writer should not twist a sentence into knots to avoid it.

More than permission is at stake, because position changes meaning. Put the adverb beside the verb it describes and the sentence is clear; shunt it in front of the whole phrase and a reader cannot tell what was quick, the deciding or the leaving.

The most famous split in English belongs to Star Trek, whose crew boldly goes where nobody has gone before. The 1966 series said no man, and the crew of the later series said no one.

Example: 'She promised to never speak of it again.' Move never outside the infinitive and the promise either turns stiff or starts describing the promising instead of the speaking.
zombie-rule-never-split-an-infinitive.title: Zombie Rule: Never Split an Infinitive
